$$
\sqrt{5}(1-2{sin}^{2}⁡{42}^{∘})
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x={42}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1-2{sin}^{2}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot {42}^{∘})=\operatorname{cos}⁡{84}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}(1-2{sin}^{2}⁡{42}^{∘}) & =\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡{84}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186344972 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "204b7397-7f5c-5030-80fc-591a56bfcf47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186342504} {:answer/id #uuid "2c72c70c-d4d1-5423-a197-7c87f8c25db4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186342611} {:answer/id #uuid "397acd27-9340-5da7-b993-a94dc5cdfb94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186342710} {:answer/id #uuid "5f117df8-418a-5605-9136-a53d6658af50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186343040} {:answer/id #uuid "6adbc01f-454b-5884-bf45-1838dd101ba8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186343149}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342710} :answer-field/id #uuid "aae57d48-55b5-5a1f-8dc9-556896931748" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344792}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e8e88b3f-3c2d-5ee4-b86c-d4867f649b19" :question/math-academy-id "q-7470" :question/problem "Find the exact value of ${cos}^{2}⁡({75}^{∘})-{sin}^{2}⁡({75}^{∘}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186344985 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5858d43e-f292-5d63-8709-e30e7df20cc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+x+C" :db/id 17592186342977} {:answer/id #uuid "9345f7e0-2907-5f48-af5a-2bbff506efd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+x+C" :db/id 17592186343525} {:answer/id #uuid "9b9f0232-d74b-5d7b-991f-f57d6fe4c8c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{x}{2}+C" :db/id 17592186343610} {:answer/id #uuid "d6b8217a-3e19-5574-8d67-40259fa7c5b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+2x+C" :db/id 17592186344122} {:answer/id #uuid "e95e1702-57d0-5817-843b-2085a3f3e365" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{x}{2}+C" :db/id 17592186344280}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343610} :answer-field/id #uuid "a2c3d901-8a89-5e9a-937c-69dec1ea7ab6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344780}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "71d110f5-4e00-5a57-9069-89b391b2cc70" :question/math-academy-id "q-74787" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int {cos}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =3x$, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡3x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cos}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{1}{2}x+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{x}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345044 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "38d0a784-5fd9-5dda-99ca-883f51f6abc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+\,j+\,k" :db/id 17592186342706} {:answer/id #uuid "4933b0e6-8fdb-5bb1-8870-15d7f9408f36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k" :db/id 17592186342840} {:answer/id #uuid "6e0cb831-d862-599e-8e7e-32ee3a3b5666" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+\sqrt{2}\,j+\,k" :db/id 17592186343184} {:answer/id #uuid "9a57d9c1-5236-5f0d-9b61-6285b27fe930" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-2\,j+\,k" :db/id 17592186343596} {:answer/id #uuid "b7bdd1ba-65a0-5e2f-abe2-f90a4069f498" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\,i+\sqrt{2}\,j+\,k" :db/id 17592186343850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342840} :answer-field/id #uuid "ea8a09a2-53d5-50df-85c4-266c0287b22d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344901}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "52e03100-7b68-59b1-97e7-23738a101a16" :question/math-academy-id "q-75198" :question/problem "Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡t\,j+\,k \\ {r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,j+\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$  is  $\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k.$"} {:db/id 17592186345062 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33866f64-1510-59e1-bc70-4f67d31cce9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta )" :db/id 17592186342673} {:answer/id #uuid "d04bf2fb-fce7-5faa-ae83-6b24753b85f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{csc}^{2}⁡(\theta )" :db/id 17592186344067} {:answer/id #uuid "f0ca02f7-e657-5790-8ecc-cc7960736bc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta )" :db/id 17592186344353} {:answer/id #uuid "f39296c6-cbb8-58da-954a-e372ded44acc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta )" :db/id 17592186344381} {:answer/id #uuid "f5e9ec94-68ca-508d-a569-9bbd35ef59f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta )" :db/id 17592186344403}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342673} :answer-field/id #uuid "41f27771-372d-52a9-ab4c-cf748b229432" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344599}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0508c3c2-abfc-50ef-9ddd-8886bbc66cc6" :question/math-academy-id "q-75295" :question/problem "Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=2,$ given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta }\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$ Also, since $r=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dx}{d\theta } & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ))}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡(\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345176 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41d37236-cdb6-53ee-ae81-dc11f5d0e79b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\infty )" :db/id 17592186342779} {:answer/id #uuid "4dadc677-4324-5cdf-b675-729c97ce84df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,-1)" :db/id 17592186342876} {:answer/id #uuid "5c70c532-84d5-5a36-84e2-40bd34dd4357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,-1]" :db/id 17592186343015} {:answer/id #uuid "83e928db-d13d-593e-8ae9-e081a49cb520" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-1,\infty )" :db/id 17592186343365} {:answer/id #uuid "c93916ab-a15a-5a14-a0a8-3bd86a3b0e4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,\infty )" :db/id 17592186344003}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344003} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c36ad8d-8507-5cc6-908d-82f87d6d13e9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344520}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "39454c83-6327-5d97-8cd7-df542c8ec3d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-76071" :question/problem "Find the largest interval of continuity for the function $f(x)={log}_{2}⁡\left(\frac{2x+2}{3+{2}^{x}}\right).$" :question/worked-solution "Our function is a logarithmic function, so it is continuous over all points in its domain.

﻿﻿﻿

$$
N-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then, the characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(N-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-3\cdot 3 & =0 \\ 2+2\lambda +\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345209 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07c18ba8-2f85-5538-8a21-e05b01a9cbc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =6$ (double root)" :db/id 17592186342303} {:answer/id #uuid "86fafb2b-e442-5fe2-9441-ec8248f9fbed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =-\sqrt{7}$ (double root)" :db/id 17592186343402} {:answer/id #uuid "95bb5822-8bde-50dc-82e3-1e93d1a93f92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =0$ and $\lambda =-\sqrt{7}$" :db/id 17592186343547} {:answer/id #uuid "ba8eb93e-b23d-5c0a-89ef-b82668d2c181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\lambda =0$ and $\lambda =\sqrt{7}$" :db/id 17592186343875} {:answer/id #uuid "e8a2edc1-8426-5f26-bb8a-60658b2ce099" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "There are no real eigenvalues" :db/id 17592186344276}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343547} :answer-field/id #uuid "5d51ddfe-fecb-5298-be87-a83009b4126f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344648}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2bc82201-7ba0-52f3-ae7d-a7d3c009ab95" :question/math-academy-id "q-76364" :question/problem "Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $N-\lambda I:$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(N-\lambda I)=0:$

$$

\displaystyle 3{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)-3{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)
$$ as a single trigonometric ratio." :question/worked-solution "Our expression can be factored as follows:

$$
3({cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right)-{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{12}\right))
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{12}$ into the above, we get

$$

$$

$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.222em}-3\operatorname{sin}t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$   

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}+9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{25{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =5|\operatorname{cos}t| \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\ge 0$ when $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{16{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+9{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{5} \\  & =\frac{25{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{5} \\  & =5{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

   

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186345236 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a0917ea-40c5-507b-8924-1137e4b9229d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186342322} {:answer/id #uuid "28556a83-5674-5632-a7b0-74ac4c5a6211" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186342576} {:answer/id #uuid "356c398e-4bd2-59df-a741-dfdcb21b6a4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi \sqrt{10}}{4}" :db/id 17592186342678} {:answer/id #uuid "5abb0cb1-003f-5e6f-b8df-beba529f73a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186342996} {:answer/id #uuid "a44d1448-a188-5bd6-bad3-7888bafa60d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186343687}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342322} :answer-field/id #uuid "96bfae9f-8994-5c06-b70f-c7f375df05f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344753}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2db69cc9-2b8f-5c01-a877-0e37bcf27dc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-76605" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8}\right)\,\text{d}s
$$ along the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(2,4).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(2,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+t[2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})] \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})+t(\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(1+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1+3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+t$ and $y=1+3t$ along the segment.

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =1\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8}\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={\operatorname{sec}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi ((1+3t)-(1+t))}{8}\right) \\  & ={\operatorname{sec}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{\operatorname{sec}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\operatorname{sec}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\operatorname{sec}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{\pi t}{4},$ $\text{d}u=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345237 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12b1571f-f5f7-562d-80a0-607aa3516530" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186342403} {:answer/id #uuid "4c9c1e54-997f-58a0-bd84-3b903059ab31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (3-{cos}^{6}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186342870} {:answer/id #uuid "7da69662-1fe5-58e3-b0c0-5897eb5c94d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186343322} {:answer/id #uuid "cfd26a22-60c5-5518-ab97-c388fe07fef6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186344065} {:answer/id #uuid "d1097377-be4e-5b0d-8118-afb24f1f0f9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186344076}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343322} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d5e348e-6403-58e5-a33c-30c8b85d2e1c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d123bbf4-7b8c-5b08-b206-9ffde691a39b" :question/math-academy-id "q-76610" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345238 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5daa3e96-058a-548e-9727-56398515faab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186343024} {:answer/id #uuid "65d6b8b8-c97c-5abc-aecb-7e85e4054fa0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186343101} {:answer/id #uuid "7bb80056-6ab1-5d01-af98-8aaa5fd2fb1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186343301} {:answer/id #uuid "8a181e36-5fec-5c45-9657-66ff3657d6a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186343440} {:answer/id #uuid "c39755ce-fc8d-515c-bacb-72a25ce9a67d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186343959}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343959} :answer-field/id #uuid "87362288-9f29-50fe-9150-93bef3fb4a45" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344731}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5897420e-efe0-5c2e-8d46-6165bb9e5dd3" :question/math-academy-id "q-76616" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$  

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi /2)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345242 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2aa8aaac-0518-5499-9551-f3a503a3343b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186342594} {:answer/id #uuid "6e78a79c-9fcb-54b3-accd-8a3e6aece26b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186343187} {:answer/id #uuid "9ca7f4cc-2df8-563a-bc0b-51e94e0a3138" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi -1" :db/id 17592186343620} {:answer/id #uuid "a8811e6b-48d4-50f6-ab5d-acec1fa73106" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186343721} {:answer/id #uuid "e82e3491-3796-5967-a4b3-1101c740da7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186344275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342594} :answer-field/id #uuid "dc23f85e-8c81-57e2-8755-3ccd535824d3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344874}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e85bae9c-7a72-56f0-9f05-0164e98daa66" :question/math-academy-id "q-76658" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}(2y+3x)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2y+3x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$

\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $$
\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $$
\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345247 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c7eee1f5-4e67-5791-ab19-b18c7b3e839f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}" :db/id 17592186343993} {:answer/id #uuid "dbc4b0b3-3161-5573-8ff6-5f7ebe4c7119" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{4}" :db/id 17592186344166} {:answer/id #uuid "e210fd40-0385-5c02-968e-6174892fbc40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186344228} {:answer/id #uuid "f3c07b9f-3789-507f-97de-8e306b0fb0a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186344384} {:answer/id #uuid "f5abf403-18d1-5fd6-8efd-732e33e8d35e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186344400}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344384} :answer-field/id #uuid "7df0e8e5-c868-5ece-818b-a9164009ba5b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344718}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6d3824d0-05f9-53c5-8fe3-dac14910620a" :question/math-academy-id "q-76694" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345250 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b7fc9c2-4c69-54a4-80fc-bad3ecfa5ad1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186342726} {:answer/id #uuid "4b8b986c-eacd-5892-87dd-71c0d9c6f4f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{16}" :db/id 17592186342859} {:answer/id #uuid "9734c89e-bf7d-518a-b7d4-04a6d670adf1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{8}" :db/id 17592186343564} {:answer/id #uuid "e6cf1f3f-478f-5826-b35f-1d2148451b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{31}{10}" :db/id 17592186344263} {:answer/id #uuid "ffef2d32-f612-5254-bfaf-7abf41405410" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{8}" :db/id 17592186344493}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344493} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c1cefb8-a187-5530-9672-96286f591e0f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344519}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "84bd9e35-b1ad-5104-8c53-a77a665c8e52" :question/math-academy-id "q-76749" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $F(x,y)=(y+x)\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y+x)\,i+x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2(-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =[-1+0]-[1-0] \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345269 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03b38ab4-3305-51e1-b199-38867cfb8385" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186342282} {:answer/id #uuid "a87f3689-fe84-5bba-8bf6-27bfef8503d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4-3\pi " :db/id 17592186343720} {:answer/id #uuid "d3aa0983-bfe8-5b65-b980-f0d8a3d00162" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9\pi " :db/id 17592186344095} {:answer/id #uuid "de1aa7fb-2851-5464-adc4-a4c73f476bfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2+3\pi " :db/id 17592186344187} {:answer/id #uuid "e9cf79d0-b9ed-586b-801d-299f6b467910" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1-3\pi " :db/id 17592186344285}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344285} :answer-field/id #uuid "bd58868b-745b-56ac-b2ef-470bcfd13fd0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344826}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b1cf0636-8c91-5e55-83eb-9e319cf28463" :question/math-academy-id "q-77034" :question/problem "![](images/00/00547d8271d0c277de2bd1992d759e0157a80c9caf05cfb1020550853ae7b8b3.png)

Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(1-x)\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$  traversed from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $3$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+(1-x)\,j \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6({sin}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6)\,dt \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-6t]_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[1+0-6\pi ]-[-1+3-3\pi ] \\  & =-1-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345299 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0dc3a9ac-bdc8-5318-91e8-e9f4dcdc571d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "p-q" :db/id 17592186342357} {:answer/id #uuid "50a29c81-1ad7-5d8f-a2af-ab521804ef38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2pq" :db/id 17592186342905} {:answer/id #uuid "6322b5d8-1470-59df-89df-7b2e1672bfba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "pq-1" :db/id 17592186343077} {:answer/id #uuid "8bb0c3f7-c59e-51d6-9385-c37a6e0e9adf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "q-p" :db/id 17592186343457} {:answer/id #uuid "a5270be3-606e-52e8-b6ba-1a9a3ff77f41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186343696}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342905} :answer-field/id #uuid "844a5f0b-ee55-59e5-a8f8-5008969d5b6d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344727}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "acee546b-9ba7-5b7c-a744-bd545219daed" :question/math-academy-id "q-77471" :question/problem "What is the minor of ${k}_{22}$ in the matrix
$$
\displaystyle K=\begin{bmatrix}p & p & -p \\ -q & q & q \\ q & -2 & q\end{bmatrix}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we remove the second row and the second column:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186345302 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dbedfadc-d9f9-52d0-bbba-03edb6bc60ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438538} {:answer/id #uuid "5d43d60c-3622-599a-8b85-3c1e1a43bcbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438539}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438539} :answer-field/id #uuid "a785d799-8f86-537c-9118-e054fcef0a8b" :answer-field/key "$S$ is **not** a singular matrix" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439298} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c9d8d50-586f-5771-9f5d-c653bddf834f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438540} {:answer/id #uuid "42f92594-420e-56b2-8230-647afe1c9aaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438541}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438540} :answer-field/id #uuid "d867bc0f-f70b-585f-a45f-e93f7009ccc2" :answer-field/key "$S$ is a singular matrix" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439299} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18ff0d6c-b87c-5984-8531-3ab4593d5874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438542} {:answer/id #uuid "f7d7a091-3679-5176-83a5-c487d3076d00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438543}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438542} :answer-field/id #uuid "0ed5cd0c-b4fb-5dc7-b022-c94731ea1ca5" :answer-field/key "$det(S)=\sqrt{3}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439300}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a70a69db-90d3-5dde-88c1-3f25b19af419" :question/math-academy-id "q-77477" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $S$ given below?

$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\displaystyle E=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 7\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
E=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix},
$$

the inverse of $E$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(E)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(E)=4\cdot 7-8\cdot 3=4
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(E)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 \\ -8 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}E{E}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 7\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 \\ -8 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}\,{\color{green}✓} \\ {E}^{-1}E & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 \\ -8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348182 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20dd891b-d694-5499-8817-937a44eceff4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468238} {:answer/id #uuid "d5955946-ccfb-5755-8612-e0cdabb5eab7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468239}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468238} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a54a548-43f3-5af9-bb27-c37157e1ba17" :answer-field/key "$D=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468840} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91fda060-34cb-56bf-a286-798cf5974bde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468240} {:answer/id #uuid "691d2f9b-6944-52d3-b95e-6577e5ed9262" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468241}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468241} :answer-field/id #uuid "b1dfcd78-f8c3-5201-b805-25717f44d7c0" :answer-field/key "$F=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468841} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "44aed856-5960-53b9-88e1-18229b5f5d72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468242} {:answer/id #uuid "cbda35bc-2510-530d-8b17-8fd2a72ea3be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468243}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468242} :answer-field/id #uuid "121ad5e6-2d71-5c46-b7a0-42914d3db890" :answer-field/key "$G=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468842}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6cd97c58-6193-5fe7-8948-41d6f4bfcd71" :question/math-academy-id "q-7923" :question/problem "Which of the matrices below does **not** have an inverse?

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{x+1} & ={7}^{x} \\ {log}_{4}⁡({4}^{x+1}) & ={log}_{4}⁡({7}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{4}⁡({4}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{4}⁡({7}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{4}⁡({7}^{x}) \\ x+1 & =x{log}_{4}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{4}⁡(7) \\ x-x{log}_{4}⁡(7) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{4}⁡(7)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{4}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348219 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ad1b940-29ef-5bb3-ab76-b9022d36ef57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{36}=1" :db/id 17592186345436} {:answer/id #uuid "5bab3d83-01ac-56d9-87c7-89af73d69a22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{6}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36}=1" :db/id 17592186346134} {:answer/id #uuid "7b0ebee1-e81a-5755-a697-cbac27922e86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{18}=1" :db/id 17592186346426} {:answer/id #uuid "7d3731bc-0af6-503e-8640-17df73965f48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36}=1" :db/id 17592186346446} {:answer/id #uuid "bb7fa320-1feb-5ea9-b5c0-8430abb685cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{6}=1" :db/id 17592186346976}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346446} :answer-field/id #uuid "21a04564-f6ec-5bf2-ab6f-b6795ab6636b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347662}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9015a8d2-7682-57fa-9d91-2827376ba1a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-79377" :question/problem "Determine the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -5,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -5 \\ \frac{x+5}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2 \\ \frac{y+2}{6} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36}=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348286 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d91ac80-4828-5778-bc38-7609f256f1fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi -8}{2}" :db/id 17592186346307} {:answer/id #uuid "70f9fabf-c90c-57f9-bd37-d2d5daee7ae5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi -16}{4}" :db/id 17592186346346} {:answer/id #uuid "76256e8c-a2be-5150-aed9-b5b630a5036f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi -6}{4}" :db/id 17592186346390} {:answer/id #uuid "b002a26f-156f-5817-a58c-90884eedd7ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi +16}{4}" :db/id 17592186346886} {:answer/id #uuid "dc0f7fd1-5632-5dea-bcc6-d1d7077476e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186347280}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346346} :answer-field/id #uuid "329a1129-f618-5a4f-8ea1-b0458c5f153c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347687}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b1986f34-b362-501d-9d2f-c2574e803d73" :question/math-academy-id "q-79807" :question/problem "![](images/f5/f57ddfb02991296cbc0280272aa1a28e36cfed926dfedcd7b1955868cf83fff5.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\pi -0)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}+2(-2)-\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi -16}{4}.\end{aligned}

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{6} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get]

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{\sqrt{7}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\sqrt{7})}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{7} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{7}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{7} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348308 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d3f80c3-11e0-53ce-ab4f-c2114d4cd6dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186345454} {:answer/id #uuid "579765a3-79c5-503e-a7d8-df4c043db39a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)" :db/id 17592186346099} {:answer/id #uuid "6cdc93a7-e284-5327-b186-e1e3e8cddce3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)" :db/id 17592186346298} {:answer/id #uuid "a961f5ea-2fba-5e69-9513-539eefac46a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186346827} {:answer/id #uuid "d6716acc-a519-5155-ab98-db9047e0d776" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186347239}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345454} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c09e4ee-3f79-57c7-b73c-91af0a4b37ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347627}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1435ae2d-a320-5119-ac37-c350e8bda29f" :question/math-academy-id "q-79891" :question/problem "Compute the Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ for ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$" :question/worked-solution "The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as:

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{vmatrix}={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}
$$

In our case, we have ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)){(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}^{′}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)){(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x) \\  & =2({cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)) \\  & =2(1) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348339 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6f2395cc-6fd8-57b9-9649-3608dc0bc00e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186346321} {:answer/id #uuid "88a0acff-c93d-5635-b346-a4d5c66fef31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186346536} {:answer/id #uuid "914833d5-0106-5925-9d01-36c12971f17e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186346619} {:answer/id #uuid "99803c67-fd32-5477-b08f-d8f71d14451f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186346689} {:answer/id #uuid "bbc6f1f4-12df-5709-8d76-7953830dea8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186346982}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346619} :answer-field/id #uuid "687b42b0-857e-58fd-a33c-44243c6fd3ad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347786}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "df975133-1a08-5160-aa85-8a5bcf430bb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-80127" :question/problem "Given that the expression $3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ)$ with $R>0,$ what is the value of $R?$" :question/worked-solution "The difference formula for sine gives

$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$"} {:db/id 17592186348344 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "159c485c-001f-5031-b26e-f83f2bfeaf3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{45}^{∘})" :db/id 17592186345538} {:answer/id #uuid "8be5f15a-55d3-55ce-9ad8-ff6f91eee7c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{45}^{∘})" :db/id 17592186346562} {:answer/id #uuid "936ec69f-b82c-51aa-b0f0-19d6eaccfe93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{30}^{∘})" :db/id 17592186346640} {:answer/id #uuid "940a0cb2-9a0f-54ac-81e8-736d1cba6508" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{60}^{∘})" :db/id 17592186346643} {:answer/id #uuid "ca9d53ec-b344-5b9f-8c8e-a292d0704445" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-{45}^{∘})" :db/id 17592186347118}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346562} :answer-field/id #uuid "419a1eeb-4e9d-5a0c-8435-a16640782af5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347715}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c9f0ee2e-ecf1-5ebf-8f05-484d1b3df712" :question/math-academy-id "q-80138" :question/problem "$4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=$" :question/worked-solution "The difference formula for sine gives

$$"} {:db/id 17592186348348 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02915c82-8065-5e74-82a1-9495fe20c4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-0.854)" :db/id 17592186345371} {:answer/id #uuid "053a825a-5e0a-5eee-97c6-c642f5c2abaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-0.955)" :db/id 17592186345397} {:answer/id #uuid "89addc54-f82c-5eac-8aae-245bc3c57ac1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-0.916)" :db/id 17592186346545} {:answer/id #uuid "8c7af4b8-beb1-58ef-8b7a-b1c7ae4dca86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-1.054)" :db/id 17592186346571} {:answer/id #uuid "90a16488-0e85-5bd0-9ee2-b77c876e71b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-1.156)" :db/id 17592186346612}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345397} :answer-field/id #uuid "f38fa9b7-ea07-551f-b484-bf242ae05284" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186348032}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b6b79f0a-30fd-5a34-a89c-78169fdf9be8" :question/math-academy-id "q-80147" :question/problem "$2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)≈$" :question/worked-solution "The difference formula for sine gives

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$

$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+1).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x+1.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(x+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348382 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09f2172d-c2c7-5853-abfe-ac6a29fa3ef4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186345429} {:answer/id #uuid "21f5fd15-786d-5624-8625-e09b4053bc07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$A$ is not diagonalizable" :db/id 17592186345654} {:answer/id #uuid "532989f7-86c9-54de-ad09-588a5c52da17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346060} {:answer/id #uuid "650ab258-c139-5812-9292-5a57c06d5d0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346229} {:answer/id #uuid "8c06100d-1170-5433-9077-f034ee74c306" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346564}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345654} :answer-field/id #uuid "0e374479-6696-5b75-99dc-96f5e4575fae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347634}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "082d41d1-cb8b-540c-9c6f-0eb8d16da184" :question/math-academy-id "q-80454" :question/problem "Determine if the matrix

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $E$ using its characteristic equation $det(E-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}7-\lambda  & 9 \\ -6 & -8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-8-\lambda )-9\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $E.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 9 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}6 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -9 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}6 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 9 \\ -6 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}9 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\right){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348395 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11280adc-f2f4-556c-b831-fa0db135b14c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ and

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\displaystyle {f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(x-1){y}^{2} & 2(x-1)^{2}y\end{bmatrix},
$$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(x-1){y}^{2} & 2(x-1)^{2}y\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(x-1){y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2(x-1)^{2}y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x-1){y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x-1)^{2}y)=4(x-1)y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x-1){y}^{2})=4(x-1)y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x-1)^{2}y)=2(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2} & 4(x-1)y \\ 4(x-1)y & 2(x-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,1)=2\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-12.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351206 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "48b659fd-f6e8-5c26-9768-e4594193e5be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186349109} {:answer/id #uuid "5944c640-277a-5ce2-9c2a-2599e9812d9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186349267} {:answer/id #uuid "647f2c68-5332-5032-8326-41c2d43110f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186349369} {:answer/id #uuid "e146ee76-3720-5b10-bfcd-704e9b605e71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186350425} {:answer/id #uuid "e97f3c4e-8306-5a70-ac8a-0d77e49615bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186350493}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350493} :answer-field/id #uuid "6e60be08-201f-5939-a6e3-e905771b41db" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350893}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "0f9d51e4-0acf-5ee0-b7ae-a69128fd9881" :question/math-academy-id "q-81037" :question/problem "Given that ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{bmatrix}$ and ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{bmatrix},
$$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & -3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-(-5)(5) & =0 \\ -15-5\lambda +3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+3\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+3\text{i}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -4-3\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(4-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}4+3\text{i} \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-3\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}4-3\text{i} \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351207 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01c2b295-c40e-5849-bc0a-6ab90895eafc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(-1,0)$" :db/id 17592186348468} {:answer/id #uuid "9b87623d-950c-5a5a-bf68-191eabe7390b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-1,1)$" :db/id 17592186349832} {:answer/id #uuid "a1ff7f0e-06dd-5409-86c5-c1a27b7ccac8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$" :db/id 17592186349890} {:answer/id #uuid "c882bd9a-b5e1-53bc-ab01-c27aef9ae89e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$" :db/id 17592186350210} {:answer/id #uuid "f59bdfc1-0e7e-55ea-b183-dde5021e752f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,0)$" :db/id 17592186350595}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350210} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6d87167-b609-5f30-9204-abd258af2b5c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6d35a3af-0061-562b-9545-45ddd0993045" :question/math-academy-id "q-81043" :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x}-x+{y}^{2},$ and determine which of the following statements is true." :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}-x+{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}-x+{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{x}-1 & 2y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}-1 &=0 \\ 2y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $x$, we get

$$
{e}^{x}-1=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get

$$
2y=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$  

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}-1)={e}^{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}-1)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{x} & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=1\cdot 2-{0}^{2}=2>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,0)=({f}^{″}(0,0))_{11}=1>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186351215 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4d86d14f-109f-5fbc-a1b8-fa0a976df1b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186349154} {:answer/id #uuid "72017b2e-c440-5764-99f9-76f9513b9aa8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186349496} {:answer/id #uuid "8a15a52a-6673-5f9d-95a7-02892ff67d34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186349699} {:answer/id #uuid "8c155c2c-3cab-50b9-babe-50ea740e776f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186349713} {:answer/id #uuid "c6fd627c-a6b3-5cec-bc46-c9b0ad435ed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186350199}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349496} :answer-field/id #uuid "bea3995e-f8db-5dc4-a647-999ecab54336" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351039}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "346018a5-76ad-5ea5-a1fa-213af5e9b80a" :question/math-academy-id "q-81097" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is a portion of the circle parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
