$$"} {:db/id 17592186357388 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "22680c0b-49cc-505d-b640-39b44fff6687" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}=1" :db/id 17592186354955} {:answer/id #uuid "b06c298f-f5a5-5137-a64f-11f61ac20c73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1" :db/id 17592186356219} {:answer/id #uuid "c56f2b79-502a-558a-9a4b-b7f786cefe1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1" :db/id 17592186356391} {:answer/id #uuid "c64dca73-1238-570f-b0b7-e5d11849a95f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}=1" :db/id 17592186356399} {:answer/id #uuid "dea6991c-28a8-5127-88cd-ffdb67048bde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}=1" :db/id 17592186356615}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356219} :answer-field/id #uuid "901e195c-2e6b-5185-aa4e-523fc5dd6d43" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357173}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3a4b9c8c-c15f-596b-bd8f-650fb45e33f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-89293" :question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{25} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357398 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "290f4389-144e-58ae-8aa0-f8779961574c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186355007} {:answer/id #uuid "426fd857-13b1-5ab3-9758-9722e35fc330" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186355251} {:answer/id #uuid "435fb70d-dab8-537c-a107-ef7870828b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186355266} {:answer/id #uuid "994c1016-eda3-584d-9ca2-ccfb245592f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356025} {:answer/id #uuid "ee2df7b5-bcfb-56b5-bfec-d5975826e4f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186356741}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186355266} :answer-field/id #uuid "9f55dc89-7192-5755-9048-0d366538fc46" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357204}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "761e0b9c-f7fe-532d-9428-c3e7936605ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-89427" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-4-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(-4)) & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24) & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +6)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-6)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+8{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186357406 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08d4ca98-41ae-5a84-a4f3-60a0ae49ed37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le 1" :db/id 17592186354744} {:answer/id #uuid "62ab3ab7-a3dc-58fe-9cb8-114e0face2bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge 0" :db/id 17592186355544} {:answer/id #uuid "68f3defe-419c-5de5-af73-2b9b599976d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge -1" :db/id 17592186355590} {:answer/id #uuid "d8e73f3f-f681-5308-8e58-da638ccaace0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le 0" :db/id 17592186356567} {:answer/id #uuid "f7c71b29-2cac-5769-a18c-40132f0235a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge 2" :db/id 17592186356825}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186354744} :answer-field/id #uuid "175dcfb8-dccf-5e1d-af7e-1ba429868a56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186356956}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f5f42eae-66ad-5bef-a8dd-b0f6039d3139" :question/math-academy-id "q-89562" :question/problem "Solve the inequality

$$
(3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4)(x-1)\le 0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the factor $3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4$ is always positive. We know this because

$$
0\le {cos}^{2}⁡x\le 1\,⇒\,4\le 3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4\le 7.
$$

Since $3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4$ is always positive, we can divide both sides of the inequality by this quantity. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4)(x-1)}{3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4} & \le \frac{0}{3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4} \\ x-1 & \le 0 \\ x & \le 1.\end{aligned}

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the factor $2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3$ is always negative. We know this because

$$
0\le {sin}^{2}⁡x\le 1\,⇒\,-3\le 2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3\le -1.

Since $2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3$ is always negative, we can multiply both sides of the inequality by this quantity, but we have to remember to flip the sign of the inequality. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3} & >\frac{4-3x}{2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3} \\ (2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3)\cdot \frac{x+2}{2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3} & <(2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3)\cdot \frac{4-3x}{2{sin}^{2}⁡x-3} \\ x+2 & <4-3x \\ 4x & <2 \\ x & <\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357417 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "090d17ce-a478-575d-a5d0-85b0bd445b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}=1" :db/id 17592186354748} {:answer/id #uuid "5a9a12ae-99dd-59a5-a067-ec2deeab6f1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1" :db/id 17592186355463} {:answer/id #uuid "b5e8c42d-caa6-5a7b-92f5-a2039702849e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-{x}^{2}=1" :db/id 17592186356262} {:answer/id #uuid "ccc78256-1b20-5f77-87a8-22bc85f61a9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-{x}^{2}=1" :db/id 17592186356453} {:answer/id #uuid "d7039fd6-8b59-5070-980e-e774b2d65c56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}=1" :db/id 17592186356544}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356262} :answer-field/id #uuid "a39626b6-50d1-5e73-9661-3ae2129431d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357214}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7a2f9af9-e452-5059-98bf-392c4d9486d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-89778" :question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Squaring the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ {x}^{2} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ {x}^{2}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-{x}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357466 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "eb85e8eb-30f1-5e30-88c6-2582220a10a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186452796}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bd483d10-bcb0-5d3a-aec6-2a397c70d709" :question/math-academy-id "q-90699" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+16y=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's check each statement:

- To determine whether ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute ${y}_{1}$ and its derivatives into the equation.

First, we find the first and second derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation. We get

$$
-16\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+16(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x)=0.\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{1}$ is a solution to the equation, and therefore statement “${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x$ is a solution to the equation” is true.

- Similarly, we compute the derivatives of ${y}_{2}$ and substitute to the equation. Computing the derivatives yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation. We get

$$
-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+16(\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)=0.\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{2}$ is a solution to the equation, and therefore statement “${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ is a solution to the equation” is true.

- So, both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian.

The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{vmatrix}={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡4x{(\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)}^{′}-{(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x)}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x)-(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\operatorname{sin}⁡4x \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡4x+{sin}^{2}⁡4x) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian is not equal to $0,$ the functions are linearly independent, hence $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4x$  is the general solution.

Therefore, statement “The general solution of the equation is $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$” is true."} {:db/id 17592186357490 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "320f4b21-2707-5091-a2f6-3f46b3db3db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{sec}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186355103} {:answer/id #uuid "732019b1-4135-57f2-b0d0-0be5c43e75f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{tan}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186355678} {:answer/id #uuid "7905340a-4ac8-558d-bb3d-307b21001f47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B" :db/id 17592186355722} {:answer/id #uuid "a886961d-560b-5f03-a7b4-90a1a7508fea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186356157} {:answer/id #uuid "e1d7e1eb-54ff-5d68-969e-6e99529e477b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Bx\operatorname{cos}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186356637}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356157} :answer-field/id #uuid "296c90ca-5225-52de-bd8b-f92f0038d08f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186356985}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8c4c99c3-e164-55a4-8452-aa0c671a6241" :question/math-academy-id "q-90911" :question/problem "Given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}+9y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation, and write down the general solution." :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-3u\operatorname{sin}⁡3x \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-6{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x-9u\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-6{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x-9u\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+9u\operatorname{cos}⁡3x & =0 \\ {u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-6{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x & =0 \\ {u}^{″} & =6{u}^{′}\operatorname{tan}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=6w\operatorname{tan}⁡3x.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{sec}^{2}⁡3x.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{sec}^{2}⁡3x\,⟹\,u=\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡3x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u\operatorname{cos}⁡3x$ becomes 

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x(\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡3x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Setting ${c}_{1}=3$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x(\operatorname{tan}⁡3x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Finally, because $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=3\ne 0,$ we know that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent (you should verify this calculation yourself).

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357534 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2051fff6-2f3a-5e5e-b5d9-ae7de302011e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186354937} {:answer/id #uuid "22aee836-771a-55e1-8f2c-029a5d0a9446" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186354960} {:answer/id #uuid "be887be2-ab4d-5a29-a18d-f9d8b2b1cac8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186356333} {:answer/id #uuid "e07a8a78-8538-524b-b712-30916e6023e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186356628} {:answer/id #uuid "f9ef0e8f-b870-56da-acfd-01bfff3b82f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356849}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356333} :answer-field/id #uuid "acbec841-be59-5008-a463-fc0d444c27d2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357233}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "172d8100-18cc-569e-9d95-d342ebc00693" :question/math-academy-id "q-9296" :question/problem "The unit square $D$ has vertices $(1,0),(0,0),(0,1),(1,1).$ What is the area of the image of $D$ under the action of the linear transformation $T$ with the standard matrix $T,$ given below?

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region:

![](images/3c/3cbf4ce4422e043cedb73e9b10bba11e9cb1e64352ff182eff8aaa0046c4e8f3.png)

Recall that for any linear transformation $T,$ we have the following connection between the area of $D$ and the area of the image $T(D)$ under the action of $T:$

$$
\text{Area}(T(D))=|det(T)|\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

From the diagram, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=1\cdot 1=1.
$$

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we get 

$$
det(T)=1\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 1=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(D)) & =|det(T)|\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =|\,2\,|\cdot 1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357540 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "024cb00d-23a5-5998-a7e2-0ef6f494abe6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186354676} {:answer/id #uuid "35ac62bd-1fa9-5ff6-bc3a-d5415133874f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2" :db/id 17592186355149} {:answer/id #uuid "4ff56156-dec0-5625-887c-a6a00810f413" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1" :db/id 17592186355376} {:answer/id #uuid "5045dc71-23e2-5c2f-aeb5-cf26fed94158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1" :db/id 17592186355380} {:answer/id #uuid "d787633f-7310-59a3-a889-9935ea02f4fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1}{2}" :db/id 17592186356550}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356550} :answer-field/id #uuid "742646f8-b0b0-5de6-aa67-6e561c90e6e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357124}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dc356c61-c382-5786-b505-51f9c59fb0a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-92998" :question/problem "Find the root of $f(x)=4{e}^{2x-1}-8.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
4{e}^{2x-1}-8=0
$$

First, we isolate the term with the variable exponent by adding $8$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2x-1}-8 & =0 \\ 4{e}^{2x-1}-\cancel{8}+\cancel{8} & =0+8 \\ 4{e}^{2x-1} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing both sides by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2x-1} & =8 \\ {e}^{2x-1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then we take $ln$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x-1} & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ 2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ 2x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357542 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bcc042b-1839-56d7-83a9-ee3af4a2efdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186354771} {:answer/id #uuid "39fb6fc1-acf4-5465-ad43-f7adda6a4db0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-66" :db/id 17592186355187} {:answer/id #uuid "7bb00612-1e81-5f02-98fa-5dcc7496952f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "23" :db/id 17592186355753} {:answer/id #uuid "acf76c9e-1397-530c-be70-0c988c3a6351" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186356193} {:answer/id #uuid "ebb99e9d-ea9c-558f-bb17-3b1099f8d9e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "66" :db/id 17592186356722}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356722} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ef80a2e-fde7-58ac-9658-7c6f6a06ef97" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "59864426-00bd-5d3f-88fd-eb20e5c838df" :question/math-academy-id "q-9309" :question/problem "![](images/bd/bd50e99a129b1d6a2c6b73145dbf68681bc92a3cef0ca8e743b63cf96c9afafc.png)

Consider the shaded region $D$ shown above. What is the area of the image of $D$ under the action of the linear transformation $T$ with the standard matrix $T,$ given below?

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=-3$ and $det(A)=2$” is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-3$ and 

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}=2.
$$

- Statements “${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite” and “$A$ is negative-definite” are true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-3<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}=2>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=-6$ and $det(A)<0$” is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-6$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}-6 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-3)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-6 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-3)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite” is false, while statement “$A$ is negative-definite” is true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-6<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}-6 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{vmatrix}=2>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-6<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${a}_{11}=-6$ and $det(A)<0$”; “$A$ is negative-definite” only."} {:db/id 17592186360535 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7120b822-0ff6-547d-b7c2-2241a49aca6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358738} {:answer/id #uuid "7d848135-2b15-5316-9a46-e4e3b36ec08b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358845} {:answer/id #uuid "811e3aba-e8b3-5975-bf14-431f1c3fe93e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358879} {:answer/id #uuid "9029ca1e-4b6a-555a-8f91-25f0d427d82f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186359010} {:answer/id #uuid "a1b0a061-fad6-5c22-b008-8d6182556cb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186359162}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359010} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d76e27a-bad6-5130-9b46-77d20a6d4839" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360203}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4970bf30-0b07-5dcd-b3de-478f21daf6db" :question/math-academy-id "q-94999" :question/problem "Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360563 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2dce7e8f-7060-53e3-85cb-4987af63f4e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1" :db/id 17592186358164} {:answer/id #uuid "6202b197-e3e5-5891-8722-848e41ddd428" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{r}{2}" :db/id 17592186358606} {:answer/id #uuid "8bc5a7fb-705f-5c74-b33e-9a9c4a94bf6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2r" :db/id 17592186358965} {:answer/id #uuid "e6251725-fa38-5c2d-a0b0-c05928f16370" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{r}" :db/id 17592186359789} {:answer/id #uuid "e704bf2b-93ca-5b8f-8349-92ea61dd3fa5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186359797}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359789} :answer-field/id #uuid "5cbcd748-fe7e-5cef-acf6-5edffcf9bb9e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360136}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b3f6701f-c993-5ff2-926d-7219617af2de" :question/math-academy-id "q-95109" :question/problem "Given that $w(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\left(\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\left(\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360564 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c5cf6f4-8993-5a59-935b-fbd20502b0fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358151} {:answer/id #uuid "51d099de-8e46-57d2-b3a9-1bf43d6107d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2r{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358456} {:answer/id #uuid "5c370ba9-4b6a-5155-8e84-b69d91cecfd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )" :db/id 17592186358553} {:answer/id #uuid "6b781cf2-8fa4-56d4-825d-5429ed24f588" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358695} {:answer/id #uuid "abad9f8c-0b50-5c33-9de5-9335756322a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )" :db/id 17592186359228}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358151} :answer-field/id #uuid "e5464eca-9902-5070-94ce-68bcd1dd8713" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360403}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5bc0127e-5521-50db-8fdb-586719893922" :question/math-academy-id "q-95112" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +0\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360574 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52cf3c7c-f856-5e1a-893d-423bede6de59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358463} {:answer/id #uuid "8d6451f3-ba0d-5b74-abb5-e944654eaa92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186358982} {:answer/id #uuid "a99fe949-6ed3-526e-8127-1b1ec443989e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186359214} {:answer/id #uuid "d2cb342c-cb70-5a1b-b38b-8f594ea8d85e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186359595} {:answer/id #uuid "d540cc2e-6105-5828-a5a3-41026567f180" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{cos}^{3}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186359618}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359595} :answer-field/id #uuid "7eeefd3d-0951-5ce0-8878-fb3b5684db7d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360206}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8a4e990c-7d6e-5ded-b574-687e77d66cbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-95132" :question/problem "Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360581 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12192e9d-666e-5c58-ae9b-549a795d8bed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{2}(2z\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )" :db/id 17592186357907} {:answer/id #uuid "2313e01f-d71c-5200-a515-ee826a71b2c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{r}^{2}(z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )" :db/id 17592186358058} {:answer/id #uuid "3838a62b-71f1-5444-8110-29c7f4dcb528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta " :db/id 17592186358248} {:answer/id #uuid "6d65b027-234d-52ec-b21e-4cda093023c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +{r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta " :db/id 17592186358706} {:answer/id #uuid "a2650aa0-1dde-559a-991a-ef66b1ee74bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{2}(2z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )" :db/id 17592186359169}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359169} :answer-field/id #uuid "41d8dcd8-411e-5bef-bfda-8f715f466b64" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360090}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2f89a4f6-9145-5fdf-84a8-9fcaed162c54" :question/math-academy-id "q-95171" :question/problem "Given that $u(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xyz,$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $u(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$

\displaystyle \int (-{sech}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)={sech}^{2}⁡t\,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{tanh}⁡t+C.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ -(\lambda +2)({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=0.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{0}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{0})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-2}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-2)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). This implies that we will have $3-2=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-2})=1.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable, since 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{0})+\text{dim}({V}_{-2})=1+1=2\ne 3.\,\times 
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360735 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "766e5f68-5be0-544c-8515-dad263f175e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186358770} {:answer/id #uuid "9f0728a9-67fe-5a52-bca1-2ca01901e374" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186359136} {:answer/id #uuid "9f0d50e6-c3bd-5841-a674-1c18cf3c27be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186359137} {:answer/id #uuid "a9953f9a-d3d8-5bf4-94bf-ad19496d9f2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$A$ is not diagonalizable" :db/id 17592186359212} {:answer/id #uuid "ff69937f-d101-5fa9-92e8-38b37ba187e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186359999}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359999} :answer-field/id #uuid "77f59847-0a70-54d2-a806-51a934f9f5bf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360190}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f6272326-663e-5a39-9245-c50c7e3c9d7c" :question/math-academy-id "q-96981" :question/problem "$$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the object at time $t,$ measured in seconds." :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(r(t))^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =(v(t))^{′} \\  & =(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the magnitude of the acceleration as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}||a(t)|| & =\sqrt{(-16\operatorname{cos}⁡4t)^{2}+(-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{16}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡4t+{16}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡4t} \\  & =\sqrt{{16}^{2}} \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude of the acceleration is $16\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Note that $||a||$ is constant, but $a$ is not. 

**Method 2**

For uniform circular motion in the $xy$-plane, we have

$$
a=-{\omega }^{2}r\,⇒\,||a||={\omega }^{2}||r||.
$$

In our case, the radius of the circle is $a=1\,\text{m}$ and the angular frequency $\omega =4\,\text{rad/s}.$ Therefore,

Finally then,

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ and $‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,3{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right),3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-1,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖ & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-3{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-3{cos}^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-3{sin}^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right){\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}-3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{3},6\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right){\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}-3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ and ${r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\times {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩\times \left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & ={\left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)}^{2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \,-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}\,-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{8}\cdot 2\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{4}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\times {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖ & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\times {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖}=\frac{{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{3}}{\,\frac{9}{4}\,}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362349 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c976fcb-c774-5b6a-a928-c21201481e60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C" :db/id 17592186360887} {:answer/id #uuid "1c4098d7-3054-5ec9-946c-217727f43c7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C" :db/id 17592186360948} {:answer/id #uuid "771f8cec-0e21-52f0-9a5a-63736c44523b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C" :db/id 17592186361367} {:answer/id #uuid "95e70a1f-88fa-59c0-9e4b-6e972706c63d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cot}⁡t⟩+C" :db/id 17592186361503} {:answer/id #uuid "a89f8988-51f6-50ad-b680-ba5ef6194d50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C" :db/id 17592186361592}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360948} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9a527cd-0451-548b-a626-0ef42c28b079" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "397033be-95da-5ec4-b034-439a24a48658" :question/math-academy-id "q-99260" :question/problem "If ${F}^{′}(t)=⟨{sec}^{2}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ then $F(t)=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that 

$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)={sin}^{3}⁡x.$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2x)({sin}^{3}⁡x)+({x}^{2})(3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{sin}^{3}⁡x+3{x}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)|}_{x=0} & =2\cdot 0\cdot {sin}^{3}⁡(0)+3\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362371 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26967be4-a2cf-5a4e-8868-aa0a99d24c89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186361002} {:answer/id #uuid "5d832633-d434-56aa-a657-fa22b8401856" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186361260} {:answer/id #uuid "9000788a-5586-55aa-ba35-f16411a076bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186361474} {:answer/id #uuid "92611672-913a-5b2a-8c86-57c92b5244a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186361486} {:answer/id #uuid "f45043a3-8afc-5aaf-aa21-f49685f8734c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186361930}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361486} :answer-field/id #uuid "d5ae21ee-a843-5e43-87d5-4194c828d175" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362175}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bb6d22f5-37c8-5d1a-9e4f-59c3f6e96912" :question/math-academy-id "q-99469" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 5 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{bmatrix},
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -1 \\ 5 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=1\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 5 & 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+\text{i}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2-\text{i} & -1 \\ 5 & 2-\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(-2-\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(2-\text{i}){x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2-\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ (-2-\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362373 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12922e44-b4e9-5f7f-8cf1-3de00c42e284" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{13}" :db/id 17592186360910} {:answer/id #uuid "35c03d2e-1b8d-5c9f-ba46-0bc8656567fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13}{2}" :db/id 17592186361075} {:answer/id #uuid "740bef2d-2a2d-5a7b-994d-57d03bf5b553" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{26}" :db/id 17592186361348} {:answer/id #uuid "7accee18-4ede-59e4-b3b8-f9949401c020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{13}" :db/id 17592186361381} {:answer/id #uuid "c66bfe33-b290-5932-981d-7236ef5cbded" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186361735}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360910} :answer-field/id #uuid "2e184656-6d58-50c0-a788-ce468a4978bb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362024}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7f1be8b8-3745-5a36-93d3-1a606462f05e" :question/math-academy-id "q-99480" :question/problem "$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{bmatrix},
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -13 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=-1\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1-2\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-1-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -13 & -4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -1-2\text{i}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3+2\text{i} & 1 \\ -13 & -3+2\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(3+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -13{x}_{1}+(-3+2\text{i}){x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-3-2\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ (-3-2\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3-2\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-3)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\frac{1}{13}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362383 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "742aed52-3923-5d3e-aae7-5ca575086d97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -10 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361349} {:answer/id #uuid "8ad587c3-4f5c-5eca-b96d-64e234660df7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361450} {:answer/id #uuid "a4c8cb0e-1acd-5b83-85e0-b9b1a7bde4b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361575} {:answer/id #uuid "caa1fb09-e645-5bb3-bc36-d3b843dcd6d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & -4 \\ 9 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361752} {:answer/id #uuid "e206a94e-4884-53b0-b2c6-1a2394ba3c14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -10 & -4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361847}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361575} :answer-field/id #uuid "240210d3-d2e3-5a83-9c97-d93c03a1d0de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362012}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7e033a7c-c230-5700-a5b4-d8c955024d86" :question/math-academy-id "q-9967" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 8 & -3 & 5 \\ 7 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 8 & -3 & 5 \\ 7 & -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =4\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix}-(-2)\begin{vmatrix}8 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 7 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(-12+10)+2(32-35)+3(-16+21) \\  & =-8-6+15 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}8 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 7 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 7 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 7 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 5\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 5\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 8 & -3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -3 & 5 \\ -2 & -5 & 6 \\ -1 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -5 & -6 \\ -1 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362389 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bfe9eb7-0858-52db-9dfb-831c6cfdd93e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186361032} {:answer/id #uuid "92da08bc-b94a-5969-b999-e830f9be45bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186361489} {:answer/id #uuid "d820da19-1020-5cd4-ad52-3b72b70b868e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186361798} {:answer/id #uuid "dda5046b-7496-5105-85c6-0e609a2a6b0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186361825} {:answer/id #uuid "e3499b31-131f-5fed-9b53-def82bb10a5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186361854}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361854} :answer-field/id #uuid "7631dea4-74c6-5439-9236-5c814d4472e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362080}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3e095599-c87c-5424-992d-faffcd2cd697" :question/math-academy-id "q-9980" :question/problem "The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix

equals $\frac{2}{5}.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & =2\begin{vmatrix}k & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}4 & k \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(k-2)-3(4-6)+1(4-3k) \\  & =2k-4+6+4-3k \\  & =6-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{12} & =(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(4-6) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{21}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{6-k}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{6-k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{21}^{′}=\frac{2}{5}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{6-k} & =\frac{2}{5} \\ 2\cdot 5 & =2(6-k) \\ 10 & =12-2k \\ 2k & =2 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5c3132dd-8104-5475-a04a-6ba3130fe419" :question/math-academy-id "q-99822" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{2}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,1⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡\alpha =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\alpha )}{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{2}-(0-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -0-(0-0)] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only."} {:db/id 17592186362402 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "360fced2-8218-5819-b49f-a6bdb1fc1bee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186361080} {:answer/id #uuid "9c5a24fa-708c-583a-a345-c52f3aa911d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186361533} {:answer/id #uuid "b26d0910-a34a-5209-9a33-b42495f6695f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186361628} {:answer/id #uuid "c9642213-619d-5f39-b7b7-a194e5db904f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186361747} {:answer/id #uuid "e3588d61-9553-531b-9d36-cee636d25f26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186361855}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361855} :answer-field/id #uuid "0ec73497-ac99-5d21-88bb-baefe07c1bbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186361992}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "90452d65-c7b3-548e-83d9-2c700d6e9c0f" :question/math-academy-id "q-9998" :question/problem "The entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ k & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$
equals $-1.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ k & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =0\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}k & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}k & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-2(2k-0)+2(k-0) \\  & =-4k+2k \\  & =-2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(4-2) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2k}\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{12}^{′}=-1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{k} & =-1 \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362486 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8475316c-8579-5579-ba08-41d5bb64d787" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{cos}\theta " :db/id 17592186362488}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362488} :answer-field/id #uuid "795f305e-67f0-5314-a428-976bafef3452" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362487}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5ad7c087-31de-5f2c-99f2-5a1c344721d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-167887" :question/problem "A parametrization of the cylindrical heater is $\mathbf{f}(\theta ,z)=⟨$

$,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,$ where $(\theta ,z)\in C.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the circle

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1
$$

in the $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),

since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9}+\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9} \\  & =\frac{9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{9}+\frac{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{9} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{f}(\theta ,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}3\operatorname{cos}\theta }},\hspace{0.167em}3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,\hspace{0.167em}z⟩\end{aligned}$$

where $(\theta ,z)\in C$ and $C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$"} {:db/id 17592186362499 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2913f404-2728-588d-a659-7b2224909a8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186362501}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362501} :answer-field/id #uuid "888db239-13fc-5af3-9362-ec8dfd52191e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362500}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "04b077f7-c06e-58b2-a427-71541763f158" :question/math-academy-id "q-167890" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral in step 6 to find the flux of $F$ across the element.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Flux = 

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We will evaluate the integral

$$
{∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s
$$

found in step 6 using the formula

$$
{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

with the parametrization of the curve $E$ given by

$$
r(\theta )=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi .
$$

As we found previously, ${r}^{′}(\theta )=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}^{′}(\theta )|| & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)=\frac{7}{3}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(\theta )) & =\frac{7}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =63{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta . \\  & =\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{63}{2}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362989 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3978ab12-c2c3-556b-8b3e-3e2439bb98af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{3}" :db/id 17592186362991} {:answer/id #uuid "921abcc9-664f-5748-a32a-b8cb3a3a1679" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186362992} {:answer/id #uuid "55926885-53a5-5ed5-b872-7944d1c6177d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186362993} {:answer/id #uuid "87181d2e-ae8e-5568-bad0-b0d06ff451c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186362994} {:answer/id #uuid "70de9d14-e9f3-5545-9a7f-d37446be4ff0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186362995}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362991} :answer-field/id #uuid "c54a12c4-ac53-57bf-ac59-6e5331dff070" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362990}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "05fbe250-8eb4-5b81-83cc-08a815c1aec0" :question/math-academy-id "q-123510" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$

Next, we have

$$

and therefore

$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$

$$
