:db/id 17592186363378}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "86c222b1-ebbd-591c-81fe-2d687175781c" :question/math-academy-id "q-149821" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta $ for $$
\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta +{csc}^{2}⁡\theta {cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-[\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)] \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363534 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1489818f-5ce9-545c-881f-dfa313c88d0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186363536} {:answer/id #uuid "a863d5d6-4817-5d38-861e-294ff12c8daf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186363537} {:answer/id #uuid "e8ac8a95-910b-5dff-900f-302d27cc3e92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186363538} {:answer/id #uuid "41dd2e89-20f2-5f82-af5e-e4877efb589e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{7}" :db/id 17592186363539} {:answer/id #uuid "b75d956c-9807-5aca-a281-f664d5d8c25f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186363540}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363536} :answer-field/id #uuid "674aef77-64bb-5be9-9abf-cff3f0fb378e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363535}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "683e3791-c874-5158-8d10-18c20b047e9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-165417" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{3}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{3} \\  & ={sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {u}^{8}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363541 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a620cea-c724-5cd1-81af-543f3d2c51dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-\sqrt{3}$ and ${f}_{max}=\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186363543} {:answer/id #uuid "2e0d1a43-6f8b-5644-93e8-16948f17dafa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=3-2\sqrt{3}$ and ${f}_{max}=3+2\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186363544} {:answer/id #uuid "81a5b1aa-671f-52ad-9681-35461c2b2509" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=3+2\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186363545} {:answer/id #uuid "ddc0f0b2-6ebe-53e9-96ad-e380f02b0b9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and ${f}_{max}=3$" :db/id 17592186363546} {:answer/id #uuid "eb7e87b5-ff70-5a36-ac7c-77dc99ac2caf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=0$ and ${f}_{max}=1$" :db/id 17592186363547}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363545} :answer-field/id #uuid "ab3adac3-45ef-501d-ba44-cfa5be5274bd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363542}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "48e27a98-5e9a-5abd-8c04-d1e75ddfe8ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-167162" :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2y$ on the closed region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 3\}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(0,-1)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,-1)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t+3{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives two solutions $$
\displaystyle t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain three candidate points:

$$
(\sqrt{3},0),\,(0,-\sqrt{3}),\,(0,\sqrt{3})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3},0) & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+2(0) \\  & =3+0+0 \\  & =3 \\ f(0,-\sqrt{3}) & =(0)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3-2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3-2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,\sqrt{3}) & ={0}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3+2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =0+1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $3+2\sqrt{3}$ at the point $(0,\sqrt{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186363595 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$

$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\pi )) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

Given that $E=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $E,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $2$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 3-1\cdot 2}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}cos(\pi E) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363956 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "640db27e-1b64-566e-a356-8324775e5d23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "has the unique :question/math-academy-id "q-338893" :question/problem "Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+3y=2x,\,y(0)=3,\,y(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1
$$

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be fundamental solutions of the form $y={e}^{mx}$ to the corresponding homogeneous differential equation, and suppose we define the matrix $A$ as 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Fill in the correct options in the reasoning below **without calculating the solution** to this BVP.

$\,$ The **absolute value** of $det(A)$ is {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the corresponding homogeneous BVP {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, our inhomogeneous BVP {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem has a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be a fundamental set of solutions to the corresponding homogeneous differential equation ${y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0.$ 

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=0,$ and $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-4m+3 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=1$ and $m=3,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ e & {e}^{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|1\cdot {e}^{3}-1\cdot e| \\  & =|{e}^{3}-e| \\  & =e({e}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0$, our inhomogeneous BVP $\text{has a unique solution}.$"} {:db/id 17592186363972 :question/answer-fields :question/problem "Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}+49y={x}^{2}{e}^{x},\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1,\,\,\,{y}^{′}(\pi )=1,\,0\le x\le \pi 
$$

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be the fundamental solutions, and suppose we define the matrix $A$ as 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(\pi ) & {y}_{2}^{′}(\pi )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Fill in the correct options in the reasoning below.

$\,$ The **absolute value** of $det(A)$ is {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the corresponding homogeneous BVP {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, our inhomogeneous BVP {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\pi ,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(\pi ) & {y}_{2}^{′}(\pi )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+49 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 7\text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡7x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡7x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡7x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=7\operatorname{cos}⁡7x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\cdot 0) & 7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\cdot 0) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\cdot \pi ) & 7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\cdot \pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ 0 & -7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|0\cdot (-7)-7\cdot 0| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions}.$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\theta ) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\pi -0}{4}-\frac{0-0}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364406 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bc4fe3ab-834d-54e6-8aa2-1f24a32b9e3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi +1}{2}" :db/id 17592186364408} {:answer/id #uuid "11e0dcd6-b288-598a-ba1c-229ef1490ba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi -1}{2}" :db/id 17592186364409} {:answer/id #uuid "beebdd75-a401-5283-81ff-5aa849295dce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi -2}{4}" :db/id 17592186364410} {:answer/id #uuid "377ccde4-480f-5a52-99b4-878b8324b114" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +2}{8}" :db/id 17592186364411} {:answer/id #uuid "ef48135e-5181-5bd2-954a-39061d970853" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi +2}{4}" :db/id 17592186364412}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364411} :answer-field/id #uuid "49a9a65b-096a-5622-a126-8ea061e266fb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364407}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "088ac295-32da-54ad-8397-ade18f5cdf50" :question/math-academy-id "q-76683" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$

$$ where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{4}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}{|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364413 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "49adc8e9-1dc5-5cb5-9175-f91e269efe35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192" :db/id 17592186364415} {:answer/id #uuid "e94aff50-1cf2-58b3-85e2-e76471a133a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186364416} {:answer/id #uuid "7fdf46cb-8dea-538a-974a-83bf0db567f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "256" :db/id 17592186364417} {:answer/id #uuid "119dacc9-0e3b-5285-87d0-21d3cc26e860" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "512" :db/id 17592186364418} {:answer/id #uuid "bddd3fe2-39af-5dc8-a534-e22068d4a73c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "384" :db/id 17592186364419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364415} :answer-field/id #uuid "7944764b-8f2e-517b-9311-deccaafc6156" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13c81ebd-eba4-55aa-a40f-bfa1b49cc9df" :question/math-academy-id "q-76763" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$ along the polar curve $r=4$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}256{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 4\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+1 & ={y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364488 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a248db95-9258-51f7-b1fa-a33f510f04f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}=1" :db/id 17592186364490} {:answer/id #uuid "85c02e3c-0c9a-54d7-ac41-df69fbd4d74f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{5}=1" :db/id 17592186364491} {:answer/id #uuid "e2dd69b4-8e07-552f-910e-85cc6e9b07e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}=1" :db/id 17592186364492} {:answer/id #uuid "9ddfb071-c8ee-5fd5-85af-78232f97eab1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1" :db/id 17592186364493} {:answer/id #uuid "74033cc7-4a1b-54e5-bfe0-d56a1f8b8e08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}=1" :db/id 17592186364494}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364490} :answer-field/id #uuid "7cc9b46a-c045-5728-ba11-94c45cf189f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364489}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "28555321-a379-5690-a7d3-5ececde42399" :question/math-academy-id "q-89777" :question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$"} {:db/id 17592186364681 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62cbcaa0-0a4b-5073-ad88-c02a4ba1a019" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451299} {:answer/id #uuid "375e98ca-c238-53ff-beba-897b64cc63a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451300}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451299} :answer-field/id #uuid "652213cb-11aa-5dea-a4bc-3b9c8b1c355c" :answer-field/key "$H(-1,3)<0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452497} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7b0d48c5-2f2c-5055-908e-0dc95f5f7282" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451301} {:answer/id #uuid "61b6f0c7-25e4-5be3-b321-0d0f90827d6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451302}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451302} :answer-field/id #uuid "d71cb01d-fa4d-51c3-8af9-10186ba20c84" :answer-field/key "$\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,3)>0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452498} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bd7d602-b04e-508c-8f43-638a3bb96a1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451303} {:answer/id #uuid "cafd6976-b47f-5881-a12d-13755ea64993" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451304}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451304} :answer-field/id #uuid "1a57395c-fb2f-5e27-af13-56da5d453d17" :answer-field/key "The second partial derivative test is inconclusive" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452499}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a2adfa73-7e18-5d5d-8163-694e5efa8a14" :question/math-academy-id "q-104980" :question/problem "The function $f(x,y)$ has Hessian matrix

$$
{∇}^{2}f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2(y-3) & 2(x+1) \\ 2(x+1) & (y-3)^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

and has a stationary point at $(-1,3).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ then:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$;

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a.$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a.$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivative test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the Hessian at $(-1,3),$ we obtain

$$
{∇}^{2}f(-1,3)=\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{2}+2(3-3) & 2(-1+1) \\ 2(-1+1) & (3-3)^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, let's examine the statements.

- Statement $H(-1,3)<0$ is false. The Hessian determinant is

$$
H(-1,3)=det({∇}^{2}f(-1,3))=1(0)-0(0)=0.
$$

- Statement $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,3)>0$ is true because

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,3)=1>0.
$$

- Statement “The second partial derivative test is inconclusive” is true because $H(-1,3)=0,$ so the second partial derivative test is inconclusive.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,3)>0$; “The second partial derivative test is inconclusive” only."} {:db/id 17592186364688 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e870df35-a29a-5740-b1a9-fc27a59659f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,2)$" :db/id 17592186364690} {:answer/id #uuid "3dc15fc6-ed64-52d5-ac6c-18f4a5d6f76d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(2,0)$" :db/id 17592186364691} {:answer/id #uuid "e5d211e6-d042-5039-a26f-2a692ad7c3f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(2,0)$" :db/id 17592186364692} {:answer/id #uuid "ffcc138d-043f-51f3-9bd9-aad344676fad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(1,2)$" :db/id 17592186364693} {:answer/id #uuid "1188a71b-6d30-5d7c-b671-eeb3e30204cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(2,0)$" :db/id 17592186364694}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364692} :answer-field/id #uuid "a892e43b-67a8-5cd6-aed3-b41a3dd2b871" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364689}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "265e39ea-f8c9-5146-9ac4-7988205838c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-105284" :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4,$ and determine which of the following statements is true." :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-4 & 6y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-4 &=0 \\ 6y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $x,$ we get

$$
2x-4=0\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get

$$
6y=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Hence, $(2,0)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-4)=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6y)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-4)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6y)=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,0),$ we get

$$
H(2,0)=det({f}^{″}(2,0))=2\cdot 6-{0}^{2}=12>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,0)=({f}^{″}(2,0))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(2,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186364866 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "75756de3-5c1f-5955-8db2-89d226263642" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186364868} {:answer/id #uuid "4b2876ba-2ba4-593c-9397-71488e2f55d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{tan}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186364869} {:answer/id #uuid "a57c8bbc-e95b-5e44-be39-723db5f0b118" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{cot}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186364870} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1f8a2b-ff00-560f-94e4-c6bb08d2814f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186364871} {:answer/id #uuid "efb7e73a-242b-51ec-9190-fbce20ab0282" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186364872}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364868} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ba32c0f-6d3e-59b1-898e-596a205d15ee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364867}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6f8e46a0-630b-5787-bb29-6f4d59cfd7d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-114445" :question/problem "$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,z)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=25.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the ellipse

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,y)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}=16.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the ellipse

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,y)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $4{x}^{2}+25{z}^{2}=100.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the ellipse

since

Since the determinant of the matrix is $70,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}} & =\lim_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]}^{′}}{{[{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}]}^{′}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{-{csc}^{2}⁡x}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\cancel{-{csc}^{2}⁡x}}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}\cancel{(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365838 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dcbadc4d-68d4-5b2e-8a19-24d686fb203c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186365840} {:answer/id #uuid "c7be6b70-d97a-5959-9631-b0fe42eb9053" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186365841} {:answer/id #uuid "253de1fe-1656-58bc-bedc-0568a43339d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186365842} {:answer/id #uuid "3e81fea3-115b-5200-a07a-e08f03e2a610" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186365843} {:answer/id #uuid "69b63e1e-b1e6-5fc7-aa61-83e97ec66410" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186365844}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365841} :answer-field/id #uuid "03f7cc94-79fe-5bb1-ba6b-3fb8a70d42df" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365839}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ef53f269-67ef-5838-bc87-40dccf2bfbcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-338526" :question/problem "Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+2y={e}^{x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=R{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+g(x),
$$

where $R$ and $Q$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′} &=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is
$f(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=R{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ and our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dx & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,du \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|.\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{e}^{2x}}\,dx \\  & =\int dx \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =R{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,+\underbrace{\,{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|+x{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365942 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "97309906-dff0-599d-b092-0740a0732b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-4x}" :db/id 17592186365944} {:answer/id #uuid "833af303-c46f-5b0d-8a79-139d161c6a97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{-4x}" :db/id 17592186455139}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455139} :answer-field/id #uuid "f5699544-5216-55d0-b396-9487609e9ee4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365943}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "593a3349-a7fc-5c8f-8d89-90616a43f4a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343757" :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}+4y=f(x),\,y(0)=1
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $3$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$  
{{field-1}} 
$$
\displaystyle +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+4y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+4y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=1.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{-4(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 1 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-4x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼{e}^{-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365945 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21b93f35-5863-505d-95aa-0b03a081a02c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{e}^{5x-15}" :db/id 17592186365947} {:answer/id #uuid "373fbf8e-f9c5-58a2-82ab-389c0f096a7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2e^{5x-15}" :db/id 17592186454989}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186454989} :answer-field/id #uuid "2f550799-2c78-5c0d-95ef-a64651fc88f0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365946}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3a5b1020-667d-5b46-950b-9e388e936e0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-343942" :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}-5y=f(x),\,y(3)=-2
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $4$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(3)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$   
{{field-1}} 
$$
\displaystyle +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x))
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}-5y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}-5y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{5x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(3)=-2.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =A{e}^{5(3)}+{y}_{p}(3) \\ -2 & =A{e}^{15}+0 \\ A & =-2{e}^{-15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=(-2{e}^{-15}){e}^{5x}=-2{e}^{5x-15}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-2{e}^{5x-15}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365948 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a7a87f86-90b0-5b7d-9095-19d6fbf68ef5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186365950} {:answer/id #uuid "59abbacc-a27b-5a19-ac83-400c63f14c79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186365951} {:answer/id #uuid "6f06faa6-96dc-5bf0-bb0f-d24428537c3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186365952} {:answer/id #uuid "7f76102e-5080-58eb-93bc-ef21e4f0b0dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-5-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n})" :db/id 17592186365953}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365952} :answer-field/id #uuid "7b5e0295-3d2a-5ea3-b1a9-dd01a18b1b65" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186365949}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e72e085b-8209-5b57-8832-a5f8ba9155db" :question/math-academy-id "q-343980" :question/problem "$$
{y}^{″}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-5
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+3=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-5.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=-5$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =B\sqrt{3}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{3} & =-5-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186366372 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c8732e6c-4d18-5b7e-ae95-e1ee81edf795" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-1,0)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1)$" :db/id 17592186366374} {:answer/id #uuid "d80b2441-9615-52b5-9198-59bcb8ab0335" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186366375} {:answer/id #uuid "e22ffbf0-37ac-5f34-8fd8-393118213c26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$ and a saddle point at $(1,1)$" :db/id 17592186366376} {:answer/id #uuid "73b12864-fe9a-5b7f-9384-e568eee33a9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$" :db/id 17592186366377} {:answer/id #uuid "df913330-c7ab-564e-8548-6b93fa1857a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,-1)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1)$" :db/id 17592186366378}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366378} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0661b48-e21e-53e3-ab77-d168dba34a8c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366373}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "16f8ddbb-3563-5450-8b85-07ba89da4f50" :question/math-academy-id "q-81041" :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2{y}^{2}-2\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2{y}^{2}-2\end{bmatrix},$ we must have 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{y}^{2}-2.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=0 \\ 2{y}^{2} &=2\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=\pm 1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Hence, $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$ are the stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x)=4\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{y}^{2}-2)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}-2)=4y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,1),$ we get

$$
det(H(0,1))=4\cdot 4-{0}^{2}=16>0.
$$

Now, since $H(0,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,1)=({f}^{″}(0,1))_{11}=4>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,1).$

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $H(0,-1),$ we get

$$
det(H(-1,0))=4\cdot (-4)-{0}^{2}=-16<0
$$

Therefore, $f(0,-1)$ is saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,-1)$ and a local minimum at $(0,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186366794 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c502c08e-cbb1-5442-bcb9-424b6777ac3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438664} {:answer/id #uuid "003139e8-881a-52b3-9ea9-221baca3d942" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438665}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438664} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee174a06-895c-5583-812c-7c4468fa2511" :answer-field/key "$det(D)=1$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439361} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4493f073-130a-5643-b440-425f3034460d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438666} {:answer/id #uuid "0508c95e-9b72-5cb3-8464-ae610809503a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438667}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438667} :answer-field/id #uuid "495bc1a5-e85e-5043-b4d4-3fe8b15554ed" :answer-field/key "$D$ is a singular matrix" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439362} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b1502369-e88d-503e-90f4-0f6ab218c61c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438668} {:answer/id #uuid "516ece6f-6106-541c-abfc-8c583469231d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438669}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438669} :answer-field/id #uuid "e222facc-8617-59fb-b0f3-b2ffe6c181c7" :answer-field/key "$det(D)=0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439363}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2e3acb77-06f5-5592-8e02-3140d23a412e" :question/math-academy-id "q-9835" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $D$ given below?

Select all that apply.

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 & 7\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 7\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(28-30)-2(7-5)+3(6-4) \\  & =1\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 2+3\cdot 2 \\  & =-2-4+6 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(D)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements “$D$ is a singular matrix” and $det(D)=0$ are true."} {:db/id 17592186367163 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "53a1d31f-700b-57e3-bdcf-d8bd27643934" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186367165} {:answer/id #uuid "2b0d7a6c-1857-5d15-b705-b8fbaecb9afe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186367166} {:answer/id #uuid "b63c4ee3-69f6-5431-b9f1-555a6275f486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186367167} {:answer/id #uuid "cf93c5be-e087-5294-b994-d0c21eda179c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186367168} {:answer/id #uuid "4e1376b1-e1ca-505c-b68c-6701296a0fe6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186367169}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367169} :answer-field/id #uuid "f2c0e43f-5343-57bc-ad26-cbe38057ac4f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367164}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "147de4a4-be73-51d2-8d4c-4cb4de81bc45" :question/math-academy-id "q-114684" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int (2x-{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x-{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int (2x-[{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x])\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C \\  & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367415 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9ac561cd-4afb-5983-a6f4-d4eb2282622a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}}{2}" :db/id 17592186367417} {:answer/id #uuid "b95dc5bf-88d3-59aa-a735-241d3ae8562e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{t}" :db/id 17592186367418} {:answer/id #uuid "535f3c6d-b465-549e-91ca-4a2b92cf64a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}" :db/id 17592186367419} {:answer/id #uuid "c5b17d89-40ae-5fe4-8c66-1be5d8fdc9dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}" :db/id 17592186367420} {:answer/id #uuid "6d0a6633-8e0c-5c5e-964b-530af5aa51ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186367421}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367417} :answer-field/id #uuid "286f4b92-5146-53e6-94b4-5d0de177995b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367416}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "637c470e-0d8c-59d9-a6f9-8a2dca1476a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-132053" :question/problem "Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & ={e}^{-t}\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{-t}\sqrt{2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =({e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩)\times (2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩) \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}\,\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}\,\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)k \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=2{e}^{-2t}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-2t}}{{(\sqrt{2}{e}^{-t})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-2t}}{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367484 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3f3602d4-7774-5286-bdb0-42626915479b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,\,2⟩" :db/id 17592186367486} {:answer/id #uuid "a86646f6-0aea-5838-9281-711fc0aaab24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨6,\,4⟩" :db/id 17592186367487} {:answer/id #uuid "d16f8a6b-65f3-5d35-965b-7c8661d15a52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,\,0⟩" :db/id 17592186367488} {:answer/id #uuid "ed2cc10f-e116-5a70-8e54-83885a24828a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨6,\,0⟩" :db/id 17592186367489} {:answer/id #uuid "a0aedead-4663-537d-a1e2-ed4fd155d953" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,\,4⟩" :db/id 17592186367490}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367488} :answer-field/id #uuid "b7670fb6-77b3-5fc1-8438-31c45735ec36" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367485}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6c400062-b704-53b2-a5d1-f71fc8c9b881" :question/math-academy-id "q-139103" :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨2,\,4{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in Newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,\,4{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩+⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨2+8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4{sin}^{3}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot ⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩+C \\ ⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨-1,\,-1⟩+C \\ C & =⟨1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally  the velocity at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367610 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6ce484f3-4e5e-550d-818e-f1c78bea979f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{26+10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+24{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186367612} {:answer/id #uuid "cedb54b5-de63-5342-98e6-7ed2532c1269" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{25+10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+25{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186367613} {:answer/id #uuid "de5e7684-e5e2-5351-ba6d-0d66b899a3c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{26+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+24{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186367614} {:answer/id #uuid "3fa2495d-019a-51d8-b8dc-b74be91a15a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{26+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+25{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186367615} {:answer/id #uuid "e6cc5106-cf6c-55a2-bc2e-ed2e5dcfcf7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{24+10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+25{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186367616}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367612} :answer-field/id #uuid "6af1ed0a-0d03-5e1e-9010-7e07caafd4a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367611}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d3b6297b-f8d7-5d66-a20a-f484bbbfcbcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-15141" :question/problem "![](images/18/18a6f3e8c2cb509bcdc576a453d0b351caf8193039a8ef9905522be8feabdfac.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the polar circles $r=1,$ $r=2,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to its distance from the $x$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=kr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}kr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =k\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{7k}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=kr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3M}{7}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{7}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{7}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{7}({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{7}\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3M}{7}\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367881 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "caadcd75-2894-55c4-9844-09b832086177" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id $$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=-2$ and $det(A)=-7$” is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-2$ and

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}=-7.
$$

- Statement “$A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite” is true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-2<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}=-7<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement “$a$ is a saddle point of $f$” is true. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “${a}_{11}=-2$ and $det(A)=-7$”; “$A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite”; “$a$ is a saddle point of $f$”."} {:db/id 17592186367888 Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement $det(A)>0$ is false. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}-5 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & -4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-5\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -4\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -4\end{vmatrix}+4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-5(11)-2(-4)+4(10) \\  & =-7<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$A$ is positive-definite” is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{vmatrix}=11>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-7<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is negative-definite.

- Statement “$a$ is a local maximum of $f$” is true. Since the matrix $A$ is negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$a$ is a local maximum of $f$” only."} {:db/id 17592186367921 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41de3643-e918-53d1-8cb0-5b8e949652ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )" :db/id 17592186367923} {:answer/id #uuid "92a45346-b02e-5a67-a6a4-d289bad3bacb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{r}^{2}z{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186367924} {:answer/id #uuid "899dd257-9509-5c24-b797-073d1ba2f7db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2z+{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186367925} {:answer/id #uuid "0e78e572-1929-583c-ac2f-64dd21622fd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186367926} {:answer/id #uuid "28a698cf-cd11-5929-8167-bd140fb45ce8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186367927}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367924} :answer-field/id #uuid "c15c034d-fc01-5c57-ac70-f9660ec41f88" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367922}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "958d3cd5-a585-5cf1-a4ae-62a7c65fe9ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-165284" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}{z}^{2}+xz,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates." :question/worked-solution "Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$

"b5ec1be6-c77b-5453-bdcc-db467d053df0" :question/math-academy-id "q-339099" :question/problem "Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
