#uuid "07f3343a-f24c-59e9-b03d-4ce328a45d84" :question/math-academy-id "q-253891" :question/problem "Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))=\,\,
$$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $2$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)) & =({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right))\,⊕\,({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186377151 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "22881922-3870-52e7-854b-ecc965b899ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186377153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377153} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27c20c3-c2f8-5770-ad73-e02f1d19753a" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186377152} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f5b18d1f-4b73-54d5-bc31-02e516319d25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186377155}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377155} :answer-field/id #uuid "bdd08a6d-78a7-576a-936d-c7c9c8ffb4a8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186377154} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fa3e3642-6e00-5648-876d-eec2cd6aa463" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186377157}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377157} :answer-field/id #uuid "74a4b2ff-ac32-5821-91b6-226847077184" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186377156}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c65d7388-c4a3-5026-b5f7-756988e3ab5b" :question/math-academy-id "q-333791" :question/problem "The function ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,y+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Express this equation in the Bernoulli form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x){z}^{n}
$$

and state the functions $P(x)$ and $Q(x),$ and the value of $n.$

$P(x)=$
{{field-1}}
$,\,Q(x)=$
{{field-2}}
$,\,n=$
{{field-3}}" :question/worked-solution "A Riccati differential equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x).
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =({z}^{2}+2z\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,z-2{cos}^{2}⁡x+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ {z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={z}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Bernoulli equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x){z}^{n}
$$

where

$$
P(x)=0,\,Q(x)=1,\,n=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186377179 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ea72beb3-2653-5d9d-8b25-784300c8885b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{2}{x+C}" :db/id 17592186377181} {:answer/id #uuid "c734b03d-f3d6-5a1e-8be8-1613151cdd29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{x+C}" :db/id 17592186377182} {:answer/id #uuid "6692afe4-5792-5c83-8262-f136eb0d50ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{2}{x-C}" :db/id 17592186377183} {:answer/id #uuid "209b1221-ae6f-552e-87ca-df73963cf2a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{1}{2x+C}" :db/id 17592186377184} {:answer/id #uuid "55feefb5-8969-5350-bcf9-2394842ee05b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{1}{x+C}" :db/id 17592186377185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377185} :answer-field/id #uuid "dc2e285b-b2e2-597a-8a91-bd5313ac2f1c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186377180}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fa484319-95aa-582f-8bd8-3955767b1097" :question/math-academy-id "q-334145" :question/problem "Given that ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

find the general solution of the equation." :question/worked-solution "The equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=1,\,b(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,c(x)={sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =({sin}^{2}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+{z}^{2})-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+2{sin}^{2}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ={z}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =x+C \\ z & =-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x+C}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "11358afa-0e6f-5a2c-ac00-bac5ee0d2324" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}(2{ln}^{2}⁡(x)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-1)+C" :db/id 17592186377323} {:answer/id #uuid "06a6cfac-e003-591c-93ea-d82ce1a4d5dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}(2{ln}^{2}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)+C" :db/id 17592186377325} {:db/id 17592186378118 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58e1d05d-a2f3-5e09-8d60-cc4ef542d365" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186378120} {:answer/id #uuid "6b43da26-1616-518b-86bf-620c54c8e2db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186378121} {:answer/id #uuid "a1d5a2e1-e6d2-5283-b05d-04dc241dbff8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186378122} {:answer/id #uuid "6025f9e6-f794-51f4-8fb7-1bb5ecb0b78a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186378123} {:answer/id #uuid "8720da90-c950-51a5-a810-615607111020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186378124}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378124} :answer-field/id #uuid "b8390406-5f02-5050-bf92-d3f84223e121" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378119}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b55a0310-4ce8-5313-8cbc-6a11afe2e3a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-97605" :question/problem "The position $r$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,3t⟩.$ Find the tangential component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The tangential component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{T}=\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||}.
$$

First, we compute the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-16\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $v\cdot a$ and $||v||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot a & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,3⟩\cdot ⟨-16\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,0⟩ \\  & =64\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡4t-64\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\operatorname{sin}⁡4t \\  & =0 \\ ||v|| & =\sqrt{{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t)}^{2}+{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t)}^{2}+{(3)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡4t+16{cos}^{2}⁡4t+9} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡4t+{cos}^{2}⁡4t)+9} \\  & =\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the tangential component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{T} & =\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{0}{5} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186378125 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9d649da6-3446-5675-92f0-31711cc3b399" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186378127} {:answer/id #uuid "a9ed20d3-67ac-581c-a1f3-b5cdd703b1ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{10}" :db/id 17592186378128} {:answer/id #uuid "1b12309e-8f8f-5fe2-a8a3-7043a4a0c623" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186378129} {:answer/id #uuid "f267a0c2-9634-5fce-8850-f3d97d94315b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186378130} {:answer/id #uuid "1a26fd94-42cb-5f9d-a8ba-64673a724c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186378131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378131} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ffa4fe2-60b8-5f42-976e-b5f6a616663b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378126}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3942e932-6885-5720-88b1-47c6287c4260" :question/math-academy-id "q-97607" :question/problem "The velocity $v$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{N}=\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||}.
$$

First, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $v\times a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\times a & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $||v||$ and $||v\times a||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}||v|| & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(3)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+9} \\  & =\sqrt{1+9} \\  & =\sqrt{10}, \\ ||v\times a|| & =\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the normal component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186378132 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4f95470f-5454-5534-a36d-d51407090416" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186378134} {:answer/id #uuid "ec6d5cd5-b7d9-5443-a55d-8e58015b3bea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186378135} {:answer/id #uuid "c2060f7f-de36-5d42-a1c9-43252ce3f8f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\sqrt{13}" :db/id 17592186378136} {:answer/id #uuid "c4cde3b4-5d4d-5583-9b0d-d6b80c219c43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{13}" :db/id 17592186378137} {:answer/id #uuid "13621d87-701e-58ef-8091-56fa12c9c056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186378138}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378134} :answer-field/id #uuid "a7dba528-60e8-56bf-a14a-82e91505facc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378133}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ac36e732-c22d-5c84-8134-8ec4a4bf88be" :question/math-academy-id "q-97612" :question/problem "The position $r$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,2t⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{N}=\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||}
$$

First, we compute the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨-9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,-9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $v\times a,||v||$ and $||v\times a||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\times a & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,2⟩\times ⟨-9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,-9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 2 \\ -9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & -9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 2 \\ -9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 2 \\ -9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ -9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & -9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =⟨18\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,-18\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,-27{cos}^{2}⁡3t-27{sin}^{2}⁡3t⟩ \\  & =⟨18\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,-18\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,-27⟩ \\  & =9⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,-3⟩, \\ ||v|| & =\sqrt{{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)}^{2}+{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)}^{2}+{(2)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡3t+9{sin}^{2}⁡3t+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9({cos}^{2}⁡3t+{sin}^{2}⁡3t)+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4} \\  & =\sqrt{13}, \\ ||v\times a|| & =9\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)}^{2}+{(-3)}^{2}} \\  & =9\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡3t+4{sin}^{2}⁡3t+9} \\  & =9\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡3t+{sin}^{2}⁡3t)+9} \\  & =9\sqrt{4+9} \\  & =9\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the normal component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{9\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{13}} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186378348 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "913e0931-a878-5504-b8b6-00f819edf9a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id "29e169b1-20c5-5789-9178-14e4b85ea9c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-107117" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R,$ and its subset $S$ containing $2\times 2$ matrices that are not invertible. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement “$S$ is closed under matrix addition” is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ and ${A}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},$ then
${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ each contain a row consisting only of zeros, so they are not invertible. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

is invertible. So, $S$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement “$S$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is true. Indeed, if $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix that is not invertible then $det(A)=0$ and therefore for all $\alpha \in R$ 

$$
det(\alpha A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot det(A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot 0=0.
$$

Therefore,  $S$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement “$S$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$” is false, while statement “$S$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$” is true. $S$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$S$ is closed under scalar multiplication”; “$S$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$” only."} {:db/id 17592186378490 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c5edab00-2da3-5cc1-baaf-38a53c01b46a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186378492} {:answer/id #uuid "17516c76-c109-51fe-8509-d6e4daba333f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378493} {:answer/id #uuid "33ce05dd-c97f-568c-a254-6549100a83da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{2}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378494} {:answer/id #uuid "cd4162f2-f683-51d9-86f0-4efbfa8bbc9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186378495} {:answer/id #uuid "9dd307f0-6f73-523c-a203-cdb8babd11f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378496}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378496} :answer-field/id #uuid "24f97229-b8b0-5ac5-8717-387f1cee4f89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378491}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ad1b6191-80b0-5b35-b5bb-b0b81838cf26" :question/math-academy-id "q-124207" :question/problem "Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{bmatrix}$
- ${T}_{2}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{bmatrix}$
- ${T}_{3}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{bmatrix}$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u+v \\ -2u+7v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{vmatrix}=7\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2)=9\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u+v \\ 4u+2v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{vmatrix}=2\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u \\ 8u+7v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{vmatrix}=7\cdot 1-0\cdot 8=7.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only.""} {:db/id 17592186378497 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a1c40089-8dc1-5f8e-99cd-67b7a73633a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186378499} {:answer/id #uuid "166a688e-3a46-5593-af42-a3a0030830cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ only" :db/id 17592186378500} {:answer/id #uuid "51e512c9-c419-5d08-b0c6-1853fae86196" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378501} {:answer/id #uuid "3f86dd95-0eef-5d67-99d2-4aafce89a663" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186378502} {:answer/id #uuid "79162ec6-2663-5699-8e94-17de1a8e8962" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378503}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378501} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe045b69-03e8-5e78-b803-d6d4b2202a0d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378498}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9105f94c-01af-5534-a486-823fdcf9cd79" :question/math-academy-id "q-124208" :question/problem "Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{bmatrix}$
- ${T}_{2}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{bmatrix}$
- ${T}_{3}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{bmatrix}$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6u+3v \\ 10u+5v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{vmatrix}=5\cdot 6-3\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}=4\cdot (-3)-(-4)\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{vmatrix}=7\cdot (-6)-(-4)\cdot 8=-10\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{3}$ only.""} {:db/id 17592186378504 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7b2486ad-4110-5df8-bbd8-25b1073349f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186378506} {:answer/id #uuid "1097ce9c-f0c1-5872-9aa5-6d9ef401ce5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ only" :db/id 17592186378507} {:answer/id #uuid "0575605a-616f-5d19-a3d9-3c12944fcf43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378508} {:answer/id #uuid "a583a229-5168-5661-85e5-c39cb5ba12c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186378509} {:answer/id #uuid "cd398182-4f35-5456-bf06-390f361a2596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only" :db/id 17592186378510}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378507} :answer-field/id #uuid "81091068-b7f8-57eb-bb1a-9c7cdd84e5e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378505}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fa12f762-cadd-562d-b233-d0acc6275ad5" :question/math-academy-id "q-124209" :question/problem "Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{2}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{bmatrix}$
- ${T}_{3}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3u+v \\ 8\end{bmatrix}$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2u-5v \\ 4u+9v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -9\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{bmatrix}}_{A}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{u}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -9\end{bmatrix}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{vmatrix}=9\cdot (-2)-(-5)\cdot 4=2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot 3-3\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}=0\cdot 3-1\cdot 0=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}=-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186378955 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d1abf8ba-5015-5e34-9d28-40c9e16c5051" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378957} {:answer/id #uuid "7e25a544-0386-5dd2-90b3-f72b783a6d7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378958} {:answer/id #uuid "8dc40c71-4e19-5d2e-9a55-2819fdf76de2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378959} {:answer/id #uuid "837c2e94-e346-5431-b6dc-4355f5750761" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378960} {:answer/id #uuid "1728f548-b3f3-5e1a-a4ca-c1075de1983c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378961}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378957} :answer-field/id #uuid "27b09819-07dd-5a76-a6ac-f1f25cee7fe6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378956}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c347ff46-ff27-55bd-81ad-5c194a632dd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-170414" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-17{x}_{2}^{2}+7{x}_{3}^{2}-18{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(t)^{′} \\ (1-t)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}t \\ 1-t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot t+1\cdot (1-t) \\ -1\cdot t+(-1)\cdot (1-t)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $b(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -t\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}({t}^{2}+1)^{′} \\ (-t)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2t \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+1\cdot (-t) \\ -1\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+(-1)\cdot (-t)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2t \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ -{t}^{2}+t-1\end{bmatrix}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $c(t)=\begin{bmatrix}t+1 \\ -t\end{bmatrix}$ $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}(t+1)^{′} \\ (-t)^{′}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}t+1 \\ -t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot (t+1)+1\cdot (-t) \\ -1\cdot (t+1)+(-1)\cdot (-t)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions ${a,b}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(a,c) & =\begin{vmatrix}t & t+1 \\ 1-t & -t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =t\cdot (-t)-(t+1)\cdot (1-t) \\  & =-{t}^{2}-1+{t}^{2} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t\in R.$ Thus, since $a$ and $c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in R,$ ${a,c}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system."} {:db/id 17592186379810 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bf3be306-cf4b-505f-9749-8c4d421cf8bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186379812} {:answer/id #uuid "675738a1-186a-5034-b012-faa1a6463030" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186379813} {:answer/id #uuid "b2d147f9-5e98-5cd7-a62a-3b200ed85486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186379814} {:answer/id #uuid "40744a34-ee79-5f47-96a8-dad2d3f736ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186379815} {:answer/id #uuid "b7371e87-7e47-503f-b703-0bb0dbb9110d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$A$ is not diagonalizable" :db/id 17592186379816}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186379816} :answer-field/id #uuid "95cac241-a6a2-5133-bd5b-0bc96d341951" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186379811}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e3ab5a48-4ec0-5b84-8cff-a429fb97fc59" :question/math-academy-id "q-37631" :question/problem "Determine if the matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -3 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-1I)\text{x}=0:$ 

$$

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-u\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-u\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-u\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+u\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ {u}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ {u}^{″} & =2{u}^{′}\operatorname{tan}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=2w\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x({c}_{1}\operatorname{tan}⁡x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Finally, because $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=1\ne 0,$ we know that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent (you should verify this calculation yourself).

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186380476 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e1bd008e-fd90-5929-a46b-6eb5beefcf10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470739} {:answer/id #uuid "a4302cb4-89bd-5838-82c6-54ec4d904125" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470739} :answer-field/id #uuid "806ec7fd-4808-5b1f-9bc9-aa801152594b" :answer-field/key "$f:{1,2,4,8}\to {-1,0,1,2,3}$ defined by $f(x)={log}_{2}⁡x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471875} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d947b90-c9f9-5b87-b476-531e2de7c036" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470741} {:answer/id #uuid "e7cbdb42-ea2d-50f7-a2c9-539988ff5afb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470742}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470742} :answer-field/id #uuid "1afcd50a-823a-56e2-8dcb-713488e671e9" :answer-field/key "$g:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\operatorname{log}⁡x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471876} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e92bf178-2e1f-5a97-9b3f-4a1be5819ee8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470743} {:answer/id #uuid "1923c438-362f-5cba-a242-95e01f945007" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470744}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470744} :answer-field/id #uuid "299a7061-4cf4-563c-a7fb-eff7917215c1" :answer-field/key "$h:{-2,-1,0,1,2}\to {0,1,2}$ defined by $h(x)=|x|$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471877}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8d8dd107-bc43-5af5-9ea8-482dedecfe3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-105006" :question/problem "Which of the following functions are surjections?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A function $f:X\to Y$ is a **surjection** (also known as **onto**) if, for *every* element $y$ in $Y,$ there is at least one element in $X$ that maps to $y.$ 

Symbolically, we can write:

$f:X\to Y$ is a surjection if $∀\,y\in Y,$ $∃\,x\in X$ such that $f(x)=y.$

With this in mind, let's check each function.

- “$f:{1,2,4,8}\to {-1,0,1,2,3}$ defined by $f(x)={log}_{2}⁡x$” is *not* a surjection. As a counterexample, choose $-1$ from the range. The only number $x$ that satisfies $f(x)={log}_{2}⁡x=-1$ is $x=\frac{1}{2},$ but $\frac{1}{2}\notin {1,2,4,8}.$

- “$g:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\operatorname{log}⁡x$” is a surjection. Given $y\in R,$ choose $x={10}^{y}\in (0,\infty ).$ Then $g(x)=g({10}^{y})=\operatorname{log}⁡{10}^{y}=y.$

- “$h:{-2,-1,0,1,2}\to {0,1,2}$ defined by $h(x)=|x|$” is a surjection. Indeed, $h(-2)=2,$ $h(-1)=1$ and $h(0)=0.$ So, for every $y\in {0,1,2},$ there exists an element $x\in {-2,-1,0,1,2}$ such that $h(x)=y.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$g:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\operatorname{log}⁡x$”; “$h:{-2,-1,0,1,2}\to {0,1,2}$ defined by $h(x)=|x|$” only."} {:answer/id #uuid which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement “${f}_{z}(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is defined” is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})$, where we have

Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}-(2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$"} {:db/id 17592186382256 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d5a77823-c6b0-5dfd-b080-ffe4cfc11f5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186382258} {:answer/id #uuid "a381d779-2e85-5aaf-8b89-c41349f150fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186382259} {:answer/id #uuid "3cb7cd1d-1fab-5c3b-9461-a541a4c58031" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186382260} {:answer/id #uuid "f9757233-a669-5535-91c9-3301d2cdc860" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186382261} {:answer/id #uuid "af3bcfe1-d593-5fe7-88cf-00c2b3af0a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186382262}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186382261} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf58cd3e-d1ca-5107-be49-843e76215f44" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186382257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "53b328c9-6698-53f6-9c7d-d6d44c5e77f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-73533" :question/problem "The entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix

equals $\frac{1}{18}$ and $det(A)=-18.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that we are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
det(A)=-18
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{31}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{31} & =(-1)^{3+1}\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ k & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ k & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{13}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31} \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\cdot (2+k).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{13}^{′}=\frac{1}{18}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{18}(2+k) & =\frac{1}{18} \\ 2+k & =-1 \\ k & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186382511 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a54aa16-21f5-5f81-b8d9-9c8589a92326" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}" :db/id 17592186382513} {:answer/id #uuid "8451675c-800a-5b38-af7f-f845f72a952f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}+(x-\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}" :db/id 17592186382514} {:answer/id #uuid "f1efee63-0a68-5b62-ad91-dd5c82f22c52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}" :db/id 17592186382515} {:answer/id #uuid "232bbbda-748f-5578-9cc6-fc727fb87eab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}+(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186382516} {:answer/id #uuid "2231f346-b50a-53b8-9083-24d0360230c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})-2{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186382517}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186382515} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3ae09dd-0816-5af5-9718-1c8c514f2997" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186382512}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7920d835-2043-581c-9bbe-89a9298e8e8b" :question/math-academy-id "q-8292" :question/problem "The third-degree Taylor polynomial of  ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is" :question/worked-solution "To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we plug $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\frac{1}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+{f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\frac{1}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3} \\  & =f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}{f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ ${f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ ${f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ and ${f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={cos}^{2}⁡x & ⟹ &  & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & ={cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ ${f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ ${f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ and ${f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{0}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+\frac{4}{6}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186382627 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "562651bd-6747-5b13-80ba-21daf53e1cb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186382629} {:answer/id #uuid "677bd66e-8da9-5727-96b2-e59e6978ec08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186382630} {:answer/id #uuid "4cc5a71b-cfa1-5e19-89d0-b6d0dd4be08a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186382631} {:answer/id #uuid "33fb2b78-a2bc-5aa4-bc8e-8e77e75901cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186382632} {:answer/id #uuid "671d444d-086f-53a9-9f90-5c36db2f10fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$A$ is not diagonalizable" :db/id 17592186382633}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186382630} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e2cb551-0d9b-52a4-a27b-09713a092ec4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186382628}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7a4d7eeb-44c2-5067-912c-74d45de2e342" :question/math-academy-id "q-96982" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +3)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{1}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-3}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-3)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}-(-3)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ So,

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})+\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, a corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186382675 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3bb3f792-8daa-5481-90a3-72c22e1e0cc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "866dfd7d-0156-5915-b7a2-48bb304694df" :question/math-academy-id "q-99949" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))
$$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-{sin}^{2}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only."} {:db/id 17592186382764 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f60da9a5-46b9-5640-917a-84d152500b87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470781} {:answer/id #uuid "db67b4ba-51c5-5307-b54f-071736122164" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470782}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470782} :answer-field/id #uuid "23a37e11-3e5a-5d77-ac6f-dd421e0cec52" :answer-field/key "$f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)={2}^{x}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471896} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ad6ab3d1-3a72-54da-9273-f6968bc86b8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470783} {:answer/id #uuid "25b3c95f-a837-516d-b120-06235ea8ed7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470784}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470784} :answer-field/id #uuid "92fb8256-feb1-5dc4-b383-cab83629ca77" :answer-field/key "$g:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471897} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cfb43541-28e2-5f49-995a-083e58df47fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470785} {:answer/id #uuid "25f24fc0-8a87-523a-b40c-0775b54838dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470786}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470785} :answer-field/id #uuid "6060b62c-dc47-56b2-a681-49a4bebd2456" :answer-field/key "$h:R\to R$ defined by $h(x)=(x+1)^{2}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186471898}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6a4c4299-1d16-58a6-b63b-ffcefd188616" :question/math-academy-id "q-105218" :question/problem "Which of the following functions are injections?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A function $f:X\to Y$ is a **injection** (also known as **one-to-one**) if *every* element in $x$ in $X$ is mapped to a *distinct* element in $Y.$

Symbolically, we can write:

$f:X\to Y$ is an injection if $∀\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in X,$ if $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ we have ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$

- “$f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)={2}^{x}$” is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f({x}_{1}) & =f({x}_{2}) \\ {2}^{{x}_{1}} & ={2}^{{x}_{2}} \\ {log}_{2}⁡{2}^{{x}_{1}} & ={log}_{2}⁡{2}^{{x}_{2}} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- “$g:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$” is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{1}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{2}} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- “$h:R\to R$ defined by $h(x)=(x+1)^{2}$” is *not* an injection. For example, $h(0)=1=h(-2),$ but $0\ne -2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)={2}^{x}$”; “$g:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$” only."} {:db/id 17592186382847 :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ \operatorname{ln}(x+y) & y{z}^{2} & (x-z)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2})]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}(x+y))]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}(x+y))]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0-2yz)\mathbf{i}-(1-0)\mathbf{j}+(0-\frac{1}{x+y})\mathbf{k} \\  & =-2yz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\frac{1}{x+y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(2,-1,3),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F})(2,-1,3) & =-2(-1)(3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\frac{1}{2+(-1)}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =6\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186383167 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "98e34acd-e081-54e7-8906-7474b5463a97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186383169} {:answer/id #uuid "a3b72f20-23d8-565c-b5ab-3794c3660809" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186383170} {:answer/id #uuid "ac0e03ad-98e1-5eba-9adc-d9e8e372a05f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186383171} {:answer/id #uuid "ff931c36-e930-54cf-971d-01b082e8fb2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30" :db/id 17592186383172} {:answer/id #uuid "fab88bc9-b031-50e9-bd9a-aba4fd2a5f2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186383173}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186383171} :answer-field/id #uuid "9e2b0638-c536-5231-9a54-4c47809cbff2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186383168}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fcc8498e-0bc7-505b-8119-49f146adfbcb" :question/math-academy-id "q-130729" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(X)=-60.$ The matrix $Y$ is obtained from $X$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{4}:=-\frac{4}{15}{R}_{4}.$ What is the value of $det(Y)?$" :question/worked-solution "The row operation applied to $X$ consists of multiplying a row by the number $-\frac{4}{15}.$

$$

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

$$

$$

Finally, setting the expression for the determinant equal to $0$ and solving for $a,$ we get

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2x(t)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y(t)^{2}+1) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=3y(t)+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$$
\displaystyle \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1) \\ 3y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x))=\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3y+{tan}^{-1}⁡(x))=3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2 & \frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{1+(0)^{2}} & 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=2,\text{ }3.$

Finally, since we both have two real and positive eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{source}.$"} {:db/id 17592186385302 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "543acae4-f105-5076-a6f7-bfe2434f75d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186385304} {:answer/id #uuid "378a7e5c-674e-5a0c-99ca-fc8305794e2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186385305} {:answer/id #uuid "ffae6e11-3d49-5276-ade1-e877a3be8283" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186385306} {:answer/id #uuid "d3f694be-eb8b-535d-b8a3-7e58acaeb06e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186385307} {:answer/id #uuid "5fbf03be-f733-5151-ad59-df20bfa930f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)" :db/id 17592186385308}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186385306} :answer-field/id #uuid "7772a179-bc2f-52f8-b2f4-de69e9be41ad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186385303}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "95c68a92-a31f-51d9-b3f4-ba9513a7793d" :question/math-academy-id "q-344843" :question/problem "$$
{y}^{‴}+9{y}^{′}=-9\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x),\,{{y}_{1}=1,\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}
$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
y(x)=A+B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{u}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{3}(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

What is the function ${u}_{2}(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}+{u}_{3}{y}_{3},\,{u}_{i}=(-1)^{3-i}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,\,i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{vmatrix},\,{W}_{2}(x)=\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{vmatrix},\,{W}_{3}(x)=\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x)=-9\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x).$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}=1,\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\,{y}_{3}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\ 0 & -9\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & -9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\ -9\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & -9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =27{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)-(-27{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)) \\  & =27{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)+27{cos}^{2}⁡(3x) \\  & =27[{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)+{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)] \\  & =27\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find ${u}_{2},$ we compute the determinant ${W}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{2}(x) & =\begin{vmatrix}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\ 0 & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-0 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =(-1)^{3-2}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{2}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{-9\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{27}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186385408 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03936218-a08a-5085-89bd-b21159a8a2d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}" :db/id 17592186385410} {:answer/id #uuid "238d09ca-3e08-5ff2-b3e4-4a29a753d669" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡v}{{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}" :db/id 17592186385411} {:answer/id #uuid "71ccc347-7069-5697-97bd-d00b2c229b66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{{cos}^{2}⁡u}" :db/id 17592186385412} {:answer/id #uuid "972dd51b-f2ed-5cc0-a383-aec169b7a34c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}-\operatorname{cos}⁡v" :db/id 17592186385413} {:answer/id #uuid "ede2af95-8e48-5ae2-8728-186263d78888" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2{cos}^{2}⁡v}{{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡v" :db/id 17592186385414}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186385410} :answer-field/id #uuid "46c8b93f-fcc0-528b-abf0-be921590f6fd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186385409}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b88d393d-4f24-5726-a4c5-591ca47c0041" :question/math-academy-id "q-38241" :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}v\operatorname{tan}\left(\frac{u}{2}\right) \\ \operatorname{sin}v\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $$
\displaystyle x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)
$$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(u/2)} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right) \\ \,0\, & \,\text{ }\text{ }\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "03936218-a08a-5085-89bd-b21159a8a2d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}" :db/id 17592186385410} - The operation ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3}.

- The operation ${R}_{5}:={R}_{5}+(-3){R}_{1}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{4}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{4}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{1}{3},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{1}{3}$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $\frac{1}{3}.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =\frac{1}{3}det(X) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 39 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186385571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4dba8559-0132-5214-a523-39faf0ee84e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-42" :db/id 17592186385573} {:answer/id #uuid "5c3492ed-9532-5e7f-9660-d7372420dadf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186385574} {:answer/id #uuid "61e4d41c-e3fc-5164-bd61-99321ffd812a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "84" :db/id 17592186385575} {:answer/id #uuid "7c95e153-52fb-5e32-82f7-a535998522aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-84" :db/id 17592186385576} {:answer/id #uuid "bcf59fb7-294d-5123-8822-654918f7dc75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-21" :db/id 17592186385577}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186385576} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee630750-cac3-50bd-8769-0e87a844e96e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186385572}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7dd7b936-dcd4-5588-8ef8-d567f8396fba" :question/math-academy-id "q-72751" :question/problem "Suppose $Y$ is a $9\times 9$ matrix and $det(Y)=84.$ The matrix $Z$ is obtained from $Y$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{3}↔{R}_{7}$ and ${R}_{6}:={R}_{6}+\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}.$ What is the value of $det(Z)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.
