What is the $1$st component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y={x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)={x}^{2},$ and 

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f={x}^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨2{x}^{3},\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186401302 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9e70215a-59ba-5fc4-8869-08fd079debf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{2}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v" :db/id 17592186401304} {:answer/id #uuid "2e6baa46-2362-5360-8c5f-7031d62e1411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡v" :db/id 17592186401305} {:answer/id #uuid "7adad8b8-d3ef-52ef-b487-e4018ac1507b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{cos}^{2}⁡(u-v)\operatorname{cos}⁡v" :db/id 17592186401306} {:answer/id #uuid "06bed278-63d1-5662-b5c3-13bc65e1ffc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{2}⁡(u)\operatorname{cos}⁡v" :db/id 17592186401307} {:answer/id #uuid "03678aa6-e1ae-5bec-8d2a-faf8e1de8ec2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡(uv)\operatorname{cos}⁡v-u" :db/id 17592186401308}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401304} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b627816-1293-53a9-a8e8-93bf2fb0fcef" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401303}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4004275e-59e4-54d2-bbaa-29203ac29308" :question/math-academy-id "q-161879" :question/problem "Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le x+3y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le z-3y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le z\le 2\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z,
$$

which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
{∭}_{R}{cos}^{2}⁡(x+z)\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-3y)\,dV={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,dw\,dv\,du
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Δ} & =\{(x,y,z)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le w\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-3-0) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$

"d5ac123c-3663-55fc-a172-6e4b0415bb6a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162414" :question/problem "The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{},\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 0-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 1|}{{((\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\sqrt{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because cosine is positive for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$"} {:answer/id #uuid "78fb291c-c31f-5ac0-9d77-7a2e07aadd0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3}}" :db/id 17592186401345} {:answer/id #uuid "2bc16458-ce9f-50c1-8fbf-48870b72fe4c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}" :db/id 17592186401346} {:answer/id #uuid "1153c6c7-bf78-52f2-9e1f-684f7eccb765" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{({sin}^{3}⁡t+1)}" :db/id 17592186401347} {:db/id 17592186401350 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "57815f7b-af61-528d-a997-36687ced0737" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186401352} {:answer/id #uuid "d4db65b8-6f9c-5494-a06b-92bcdce809b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186401353} {:answer/id #uuid "eb263125-4fe2-540b-a807-c4ea79034c46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186401354} {:answer/id #uuid "9709336c-60b5-5d73-aab9-35c162acf334" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186401355} {:answer/id #uuid "7440cb05-c5ac-59cb-a23c-02e409faf53f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186401356}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401355} :answer-field/id #uuid "e0797b50-1acd-58f0-8079-590c6e07a834" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401351}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ac9e9607-a2dd-5594-94f3-d6c7ba9a234a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162418" :question/problem "The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-{t}^{2}⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{2\cdot (\,\bbox[2pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?" :question/worked-solution "The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-{t}^{2}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2)-(-2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{{((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186401579 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7cd4c18b-e511-5b14-9f13-a5b4cb4f47f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-3$ and  ${f}_{max}=15$" :db/id 17592186401581} {:answer/id #uuid "2821ee27-e28a-5af2-b0bc-7da60bb40070" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-15$ and  ${f}_{max}=17$" :db/id 17592186401582} {:answer/id #uuid "77dac977-36a1-5c53-9361-88fca32b4abf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-15$ and  ${f}_{max}=1$" :db/id 17592186401583} {:answer/id #uuid "d746e3e5-aa5e-5fa1-88ee-69128529ad71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=-1$ and  ${f}_{max}=4$" :db/id 17592186401584} {:answer/id #uuid "18156a3d-068d-5e69-8ef7-8771427933c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{min}=1$ and  ${f}_{max}=17$" :db/id 17592186401585}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401582} :answer-field/id #uuid "bc59060d-a9ed-5533-b31b-311227554f8c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401580}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e7d00266-1ded-5f4c-819a-7467528496c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-167165" :question/problem "Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=1-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-2x,\,2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x &=0 \\ 2y &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{′} & =0 \\ 32\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points:

$$
(4,0),\,(0,4),\,(-4,0),\,(0,-4)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(4,0)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(-4,0)$ | $(0,-4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-15$ | $17$ | $-15$ | $17$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-15$ at the points $(4,0)$ and $(-4,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $17$ at the points $(0,4)$ and $(0,-4).$"} {:db/id 17592186401627 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0beb1ecb-7649-51d5-8923-8085f1d146bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e" :db/id 17592186401629} {:answer/id #uuid "aa5ec049-b8d0-5c17-a28c-05813122674f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e-1" :db/id 17592186401630} {:answer/id #uuid "c2d87b1b-17a5-523c-a973-f5e0ad287cd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186401631} {:answer/id #uuid "ea4f4094-0cfd-5ae4-8308-88f0b83b2c27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e+1" :db/id 17592186401632} {:answer/id #uuid "946c0adc-baba-5359-a975-69b7a89f4838" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186401633}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401630} :answer-field/id #uuid "5088efea-7f9e-57d5-8f9c-14c688a0e06b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401628}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "104d7814-9b21-55a2-864d-c61ec56f5c8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-17392" :question/problem "Given that $y=2{x}^{e}-ln⁡x$, find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{e}-ln⁡x) \\  & =2e{x}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2e{x}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =2e\cdot {1}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =2e-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186401805 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a34f86b-faa2-5844-9680-3f6951dc4ecf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{4}{csc}^{2}⁡x+8{x}^{3}cot⁡x" :db/id 17592186401807} {:answer/id #uuid "63214331-a811-5bf2-8cb7-4da5c8c1d678" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}{cot}^{2}⁡x-8{x}^{3}csc⁡x" :db/id 17592186401808} {:answer/id #uuid "2285f6af-f131-5a62-954e-164127014717" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}{csc}^{2}⁡x-8{x}^{3}cot⁡x" :db/id 17592186401809} {:answer/id #uuid "5a35c415-50b4-5005-8173-6121abbd643e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}csc⁡x-8{x}^{3}cot⁡x" :db/id 17592186401810} {:answer/id #uuid "cb8e226f-a28c-5b1a-b7df-6f312bfd06a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}{csc}^{2}⁡x+8{x}^{3}tan⁡x" :db/id 17592186401811}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186401809} :answer-field/id #uuid "f7aeb284-4f80-510f-8935-07a7e23c626b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186401806}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ee4e083b-fcc9-5eb5-9a27-ac52f9a97afd" :question/math-academy-id "q-1913" :question/problem "Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ if $y=-2{x}^{4}cot⁡x.$" :question/worked-solution "We calculate the derivative using the product rule, as follows:

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the matrix $E-\lambda I:$

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ using its characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-6-\lambda  & 8 \\ -3 & 8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-(8)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 8 \\ -3 & 8\end{bmatrix}-(-4)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 \\ -3 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-2 & 8 & 0 \\ -3 & 12 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-2 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 8 \\ -3 & 8\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 8 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- The function $h(x)=x-2$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it  is continuous on $[1,3]$ and differentiable on $(1,3).$ Therefore, $h(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186404315 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06cba355-0ee9-5493-b5b4-b01907ba7853" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "cot⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}" :db/id 17592186404317} {:answer/id #uuid "88bc01f1-e620-5d5f-b135-3c829509a914" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "cot⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{7}" :db/id 17592186404318} {:answer/id #uuid "c44c5852-2bff-553c-b41d-6c60dda93e43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "cot⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}" :db/id 17592186404319} {:answer/id #uuid "e6647b56-89a1-5a81-85bf-14ccfa47147b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "cot⁡\theta =-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}" :db/id 17592186404320} {:answer/id #uuid "814df066-a51f-5318-8a89-ed554769eecb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "cot⁡\theta =\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186404321}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404320} :answer-field/id #uuid "9151fede-a06c-511f-acdd-16c15e3d7d4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404316}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "37e87bc7-80c8-5654-8c99-e96b9d9f6c6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-85640" :question/problem "![](images/97/97c98411b3455c78c9e061cf54fa76eabfccc369e9e364a5366eb58bd5d2935d.png)

"9debd71f-7b2d-5a32-ae10-ca946736e9d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-123458" :question/problem "Which of the following gives $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s
$$ with the arc-length integrand simplified pointwise in the given polar angle $\theta$ (on each smooth piece, without reparametrizing), where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi $ ?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Where $1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta>0$, $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Applying the arc-length formula piecewise between the finitely many zeros of $r$, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{\left(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "05f34f9e-a42b-5ca4-92ff-78f343cf89ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15-5cos(x)" :db/id 17592186406006} {:answer/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ &=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{1}{1} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =1 \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\ ϕ & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={3}^{2}+(3)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =2\cdot {3}^{2} \\ {R}^{2} & =18 \\ R & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x=3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-{45}^{∘})
$$"} {:db/id 17592186406755 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cb42de31-4232-5d44-86a4-641fe9afe8a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186406735}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406735} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a979868-fdbf-5b6d-9244-57c159ea73a1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186406748} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03200264-5c2e-536b-8955-c9e999430ede" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186406713}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406713} :answer-field/id #uuid "da5d992d-d452-5d95-b843-0b9cce1036fc" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186406751}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7a8d83c6-dbd1-545a-90aa-30ab2cbbb8f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-181989" :question/problem "What are the minimum and maximum of the set $A={-8,\,0,\,4,\,-1}?$

Consider the affine transformation $T,$ given by

\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 
What would be the image of the quadrilateral shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the quadrilateral under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} {:db/id 17592186409688 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "403dcee3-3eac-5cf3-a329-0558750fb3b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186409660} {:answer/id #uuid "62a1a85b-a36c-54a7-b3bd-55a36f4cb315" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186409664} {:answer/id #uuid "77636ea6-fba2-560e-a69f-f3d2282f86f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-14" :db/id 17592186409669} {:answer/id #uuid "81cdf51b-4eb6-557c-9452-11d65bc919bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186409671} {:answer/id #uuid "ebe826b2-b0aa-57e0-a4ad-251af663d3fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186409678}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409671} :answer-field/id #uuid "1a00ccd6-15ad-566e-9909-ced57101fb7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409684}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4a80ad4c-5529-5931-9d7c-574d40c6f47e" :question/math-academy-id "q-72748" :question/problem "Suppose $B$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(B)=-7.$ The matrix $C$ is obtained from $B$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(C)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}$ involves multiplying a row by $2,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $2$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $2$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C) & =2\cdot (-det(B)) \\  & =-2det(B) \\  & =-2\cdot (-7) \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409689 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "512abaff-433d-5e4a-864f-f1df10d56d6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "60" :db/id 17592186409663} {:answer/id #uuid "7a56edfe-4461-57d1-8804-22f3e005401a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186409670} {:answer/id #uuid "f689939f-47fe-5c00-a125-9fe1fc1187ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "180" :db/id 17592186409679} {:answer/id #uuid "face2d4d-2a2b-5eb7-8047-8fb6dbd54d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "160" :db/id 17592186409680} {:answer/id #uuid "fcf8031f-e31a-5703-96b3-5a28bec971aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "320" :db/id 17592186409682}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409682} :answer-field/id #uuid "98c176ba-da66-551c-9c0c-0c257e4d9459" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409686}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "81c5993c-3d71-5869-bbf5-3e36b2df3a7f" :question/math-academy-id "q-72741" :question/problem "Suppose $Y$ is a $6\times 6$ matrix and $det(Y)=5.$ What is the value of $det(2Y)?$" :question/worked-solution "Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot Y)={k}^{n}\cdot det(Y).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=2$ and $n=6.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(2Y) & ={2}^{6}\cdot det(Y) \\  & =64\cdot 5 \\  & =320.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409690 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3f5903e6-2dfb-5988-91aa-d76353ccd959" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}" :db/id 17592186409659} {:answer/id #uuid "6d3a3be9-dab5-5f7f-8e95-4eab3b47ad8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186409665} {:answer/id #uuid "6d7bf72b-a934-51fa-b417-3e7f04a3f3b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186409666} {:answer/id #uuid "7190fbd3-e0c2-5f59-a1f5-3e49c40c46d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:=2{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186409668} {:answer/id #uuid "c8afe3f3-a5ef-55a7-b5dd-30e21d2e58fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2}" :db/id 17592186409676}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409659} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a779adf-221a-5189-a14f-312c86e15c0d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409685}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9ac571f6-6f05-5f70-8bcf-34738f544556" :question/math-academy-id "q-43046" :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 5 & -4 & -3 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{bmatrix}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 5 & -4 & -3 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{vmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that $f:X\to Y$ is an *into* function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element $y$ in $Y$ such that it has no preimage in $X:$ 

$f:X\to Y$ is an into function if $∃\,y\in Y$ such that $∀\,x\in X,$ we have $f(x)\ne y.$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- “$f:(0,\infty )\to R$ defined by $f(x)=-{log}_{2}⁡(x)$” is a *not* an into function. Given $y\in R,$ we can choose $x={2}^{-y}\in (0,\infty ).$ Then $f(x)=f({2}^{-y})=-{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{-y})=y.$

- “$h:R\to (0,\infty )$ defined by $h(x)={3}^{x}$” is a *not* an into function. Given $y\in (0,\infty ),$ we can choose $x={log}_{3}⁡y\in R.$ Then $h(x)=h({log}_{3}⁡y)={3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(y)}=y.$

- “$g:Q\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$” is an into function. Let's take $y=\sqrt[3]{(\sqrt{2})}\in R.$ There is no number $x\in Q$ such that $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}=y.$ Indeed, in this case we would have 

$$
\sqrt[3]{x}=y\,⇔\,\sqrt[3]{x}=\sqrt[3]{(\sqrt{2})}\,⇔\,x=\sqrt{2}\in Q,
$$

 which is false.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$g:Q\to R$ defined by $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$” only."} {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186410196 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1700f9a6-fd4f-55e6-a5b2-c7c162c8b09c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410167} {:answer/id #uuid "56db98f5-8954-5a74-9db5-ea9ad36d4145" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410174} {:answer/id #uuid "5fd6a7be-2123-5e1c-93b5-fa6a69ebca48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410178} {:answer/id #uuid "6f32c544-2ebd-5102-86f5-09f04cfa659e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410179} {:answer/id #uuid "8b0dcfdc-b7d8-5406-814d-16ab7d147b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410181}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410179} :answer-field/id #uuid "62b7e0f0-3a2a-5bad-a1a2-7313ccefaabb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5e6637da-fa52-5317-a60a-ab7680b44bc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-138128" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186410198 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0403e816-9a8a-5caa-a60f-9e0db37c2581" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410165} {:answer/id #uuid "2ad356f6-e2a2-578b-805e-5d220905af93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410170} {:answer/id #uuid "9cbc00fe-d9dc-5e75-8939-93c74926f323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410182} {:answer/id #uuid "c87e6493-0b51-5dfe-8402-a4a84620be0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410187} {:answer/id #uuid "fa1e17c0-a680-5fd1-840a-1550ea0d3fa6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410189}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410170} :answer-field/id #uuid "59381183-ff09-50a9-9c38-82023491a255" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410190}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f0bc9465-a035-5136-b09d-b009ddf817a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170400" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

$$

The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "11871c64-6368-59c5-9ec4-a19994f69e2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x{tan}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186410216} {:db/id 17592186410429 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "714d3c80-c42b-53fa-ac34-c002e7d83a01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186410276}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410276} :answer-field/id #uuid "b74cd008-64ba-599d-b9ba-bae5a27661b2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186410404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8220b103-348c-5b5b-b0e1-61384fcc7157" :question/math-academy-id "q-253140" :question/problem "![](images/b6/b6abb4332c7601200fec40e8b3f8e6f6f8c81004aaa92af936063625a5c9f2e8.png)

What is the infimum of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

${inf}_{x\in R}f(x)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of a function is the infimum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=(-3,2).$

To find the infimum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y\le -3$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $y>-3$ is **not** a lower bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $A$ that is smaller than $y$ for any $y>-3.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-3]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and

$$
{inf}_{x\in R}f(x)=inf(A)=max(-\infty ,-3]=-3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186411860 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50c3a6e2-38fd-585d-9e5e-4100891b13bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186411720} {:answer/id #uuid "5bb3f282-1950-5f30-8116-34225566b739" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186411727} {:answer/id #uuid "7eb342f1-4d9a-5fcf-8689-58e054ad9134" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186411745} {:answer/id #uuid "ce4175b2-aec8-519f-91bb-665c302224a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186411792} {:answer/id #uuid "f3fd7c58-8232-54be-81c8-be848ef0f965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\pi }" :db/id 17592186411813}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411727} :answer-field/id #uuid "89e7aed8-a1dc-58e4-8fb1-6b3e5ccc64a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411836}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5ff06561-72e7-5575-b3f6-d0740b1e717f" :question/math-academy-id "q-163259" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=4xy$ on the portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin, where $x\ge 0$ and $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/eb/eb8745d968da24a8500bd079638b17bc461ab2d97b93d1d1a7d6d4834365bb5a.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{4}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}4{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-{sin}^{2}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{4}{\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{2}{\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186411868 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0be1ee9b-69bf-52e3-8089-48b6079a6650" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}" :db/id 17592186411688} {:answer/id #uuid "6692c8a0-5b7a-50e2-8f3a-9789034d55a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186411733} {:answer/id #uuid "9e30ff60-cfaf-503d-a59c-7208799a6d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{t}{\sqrt{2}}" :db/id 17592186411761} {:answer/id #uuid "b0e309d6-7791-565f-a947-86bc64e04da0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{t}" :db/id 17592186411770} {:answer/id #uuid "e7c7f1db-e315-5925-b5d8-227085379706" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}" :db/id 17592186411808}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411770} :answer-field/id #uuid "008191e4-1343-56f9-9409-2e7c06d48454" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411818}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a3fef8c5-dedd-5425-a060-104bbe0a3652" :question/math-academy-id "q-34177" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $T(t)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the parameter t. Since we are given the curve r(t) parametrized by the parameter 
t (not the arc length s), we will use the following formula for the curvature

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ &  \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

since $t>0.$ 

Hence, the corresponding unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the curvature for  $t>0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186411963 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1efd96de-5d59-5c21-b6c4-f57a804edb99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186411913} {:answer/id #uuid "2bb7ef99-5504-5559-a251-067d58c0bd0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186411914} {:answer/id #uuid "5f7847c9-3225-566d-a4bb-dbc66736309d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186411923} {:answer/id #uuid "ca4dd63f-7252-5bf2-9499-144f36222c27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186411945} {:answer/id #uuid "e1001e71-dfc2-59ca-a3c7-8d9e00835d22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186411947}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411945} :answer-field/id #uuid "93fee275-10ef-55f5-b6b3-8793339d38c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411961}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "441df1fa-6b02-5f85-abd1-1592ef6dada4" :question/math-academy-id "q-72770" :question/problem "Consider the matrices given below. Given that $A$ and $B$ are row equivalent matrices and $det(A)=1$, find $det(B).$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 4 & -8 & 12 \\ 4 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $B$ can be obtained from $A$ by multiplying the $2$nd row by $4.$ 

So, the determinant is multiplied by $4$ as well.
Therefore, we obtain

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})=\text{det}(A)=14
$$

and

$$
det(I)=1.
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}3I & =3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a diagonal matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} & ={3}^{3}=27.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=-13$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=14-27=-13
$$

- Statement $-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-13$ is true. Indeed,

$$
-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-14+1=-13
$$

- Statement $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=-28$ is false. We have

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=14-14=0\ne -28
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=-13$; $-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-13$ only."} {:db/id 17592186413064 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d7b2fd89-a660-5176-a690-d8f8260781b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186413054}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413054} :answer-field/id #uuid "757b53fd-f4bb-5830-9604-cf22f83bd7d5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186413059}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0347061a-970d-5566-8d6a-57e3c30b6fb2" :question/math-academy-id "q-181577" :question/problem "If $A=\{5,20,80,320,…,5\,368\,709\,120\},$ then $|A|=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "The cardinality of a finite set $A$ is the number of elements in $A.$ 

Notice that the elements of our set 

$$
5,\,20,\,80,\,320,\,…
$$

form a geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =4 \\  & =\frac{20}{5} \\  & =\frac{80}{20} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The $n$th term of our geometric sequence, denoted ${a}_{n},$ is given by

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}=5({4}^{n-1})=\frac{5}{4}(4)^{n}.
$$

Therefore, we can express $A$ in set-builder notation as follows:

$$
A=\{\frac{5}{4}(4)^{n}:n\in N,\,1\le n\le N\}
$$

where $N\in N$ is to be determined.

To find $N,$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4}(4)^{N} & =5\,368\,709\,120 \\ {4}^{N} & =4\,294\,967\,296 \\ N & ={log}_{4}⁡(4\,294\,967\,296) \\ N & =\frac{{log}_{10}⁡(4\,294\,967\,296)}{{log}_{10}⁡(4)} \\ N & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our set $A$ can be expressed as

$$
A=\{\frac{5}{4}(4)^{n}:n\in N,\,1\le n\le 16\}.
$$

Finally, since $A$ has $16$ elements, we must have $|A|=16.$"} {:db/id 17592186413068 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "393db834-e593-560c-987f-8e69f57279cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186413045}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413045} :answer-field/id #uuid "6003be51-464a-5fff-b640-c989db581606" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186413058}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9bc860de-458f-50fe-a95e-897939b46d0f" :question/math-academy-id "q-181581" :question/problem "If $A=\{1,5,25,125,…,30\,517\,578\,125\},$ then $|A|=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "The cardinality of a finite set $A$ is the number of elements in $A.$ 

Notice that the elements of our set 

$$
1,\,5,\,25,\,125,\,…
$$

form a geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =5 \\  & =\frac{5}{1} \\  & =\frac{25}{5} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

The $n$th term of our geometric sequence, denoted ${a}_{n},$ is given by

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}=1\cdot {5}^{n-1}={5}^{n-1}.
$$

Therefore, we can express $A$ in set-builder notation as follows:

$$
A=\{{5}^{n-1}:n\in N,\,1\le n\le N\}
$$

where $N\in N$ is to be determined.

To find $N,$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{N-1} & =30\,517\,578\,125 \\ N-1 & ={log}_{5}⁡(30\,517\,578\,125) \\ N-1 & =\frac{{log}_{10}⁡(30\,517\,578\,125)}{{log}_{10}⁡(5)} \\ N-1 & =15 \\ N & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our set $A$ can be expressed as

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x.$"} {:db/id 17592186413630 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "96beea54-57c3-53ca-9a62-26604472224a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\csc(x)" :db/id 17592186413614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413614} :answer-field/id #uuid "33b8438b-3327-575c-ae05-92d222d1ed04" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186413621}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fed635cb-d378-5d78-b478-1026e862dee7" :question/math-academy-id "q-341953" :question/problem "Given that $y=(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}$, find ${y}^{′}.$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the object at time $t,$ measured in seconds." :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}||a(t)|| & =\sqrt{(-50\operatorname{cos}⁡5t)^{2}+(-50\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{50}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡5t+{50}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡5t} \\  & =\sqrt{{50}^{2}} \\  & =50\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude of the acceleration is $50\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Note that $||a||$ is constant, but $a$ is not. 

**Method 2**

For uniform circular motion in the $xy$-plane, we have

$$
a=-{\omega }^{2}r\,⇒\,||a||={\omega }^{2}||r||.
$$

In our case, the radius of the circle is $a=2\,\text{m}$ and the angular frequency $\omega =5\,\text{rad/s}.$ Therefore,

$$
||a||={5}^{2}\cdot 2=50\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186414224 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "31222f3b-2ab4-5b9e-a782-7337c19d97f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\text{ m/s}" :db/id 17592186414190} {:answer/id #uuid "69ab6c9f-a3a5-5ce4-8790-f06da39f2e5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\text{ m/s}" :db/id 17592186414195} {:answer/id #uuid "74489a4f-0f2e-5d3d-b8ce-522969cbe4d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}" :db/id 17592186414198} {:answer/id #uuid "a14dcc4c-31b8-57fe-9ac6-4fcf63038a6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}" :db/id 17592186414205} {:answer/id #uuid "d93d225c-e122-533c-8881-688bb8703984" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}" :db/id 17592186414212}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414212} :answer-field/id #uuid "bba5b4d7-4309-5292-8088-c53e4d246dcb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414221}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a62921c3-0ad7-5f20-8061-cad8dd0b028d" :question/math-academy-id "q-97641" :question/problem "An object moves along a circular path with position $r(t)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j$ meters. $$

where $R$ is the radius of the circle, and $\omega $ is the angular velocity.

In our case, the radius of the circle is $R=\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}$ and the angular frequency $\omega =4\,\text{rad/s}.$ Therefore,

$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "130b870f-02ff-5d3c-ab1b-056597b4e00c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "72{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt" :db/id 17592186414838} {:answer/id #uuid "84d43f47-82cb-5b0d-880b-dfce30bd84f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "27{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt" :db/id 17592186414872} {:db/id 17592186414918 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02e28cc7-f7f3-51e1-bea0-158eef714f3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186414829} {:answer/id #uuid "08339a10-b80f-5555-8e33-e4cd3d9e86b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{4}" :db/id 17592186414831} {:answer/id #uuid "1263d5b8-2a16-5cf4-bfba-339ea29a3a16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186414837} {:answer/id #uuid "5773a110-68a4-55f1-abfc-418c6517f35e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{9}{4}" :db/id 17592186414851} {:answer/id #uuid "7b6ccc95-f5af-538e-adc2-b6c8fdfcacc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186414864}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414864} :answer-field/id #uuid "a60002fd-79c9-55af-8350-d15ad8aa640e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414911}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "17a6c1da-e7e7-5509-a937-e43376741415" :question/math-academy-id "q-125234" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

\displaystyle {\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $2$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$

\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\sqrt{z-1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z-1}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

generated when the curve $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right),$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\pi \le y\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right),$ we obtain $$
\displaystyle {f}^{′}(y)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2}\right).
$$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$

$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2xy)\,dx+2{sin}^{2}⁡(xy)\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/f4/f4bb6636c104cf17bcd4b25037a3490ba30b7c1380b152c33504d9015903bdca.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2xy)$ and $Q(x,y)=2{sin}^{2}⁡xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)=2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2xy)\,dx+2{sin}^{2}⁡(xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)-(-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy).$"} {:db/id 17592186415982 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "008daf1a-a433-5118-aad3-61bc2cd82151" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-21" :db/id 17592186415943} {:answer/id #uuid "11622f2c-a064-5989-bfd9-037259b1990a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-18" :db/id 17592186415945} {:answer/id #uuid "31b4ae36-f11f-5826-afc4-9e1f22cf793d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186415954} {:answer/id #uuid "9ac59834-bde8-5e44-938a-c936359f2042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186415961} {:answer/id #uuid "a786601a-73a7-5725-8042-296bce616964" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186415963}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415945} :answer-field/id #uuid "105048ab-2d03-5b31-abc9-b516f5aaa13b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415974}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9c04d8b1-030c-5d18-9c3c-13b32378d108" :question/math-academy-id "q-161316" :question/problem "![](images/0b/0b1b263baf01b692a0344388207c12d3c4dac0f49d11cd4bfa744f2841df2c6b.png)
