where $S$ is defined by $z=x-\sqrt{2}y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O$ in the fourth quadrant, as shown above." :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot r\text{ }\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}2r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\,\text{d}r \\  & =9[-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =9\cdot (-1-1) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415983 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "193323db-4837-5978-b14e-f2ac7216eb5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186415948} {:answer/id #uuid "6a54bfb9-103b-535a-a0de-5777c5154e7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186415958} {:answer/id #uuid "a40290ed-721f-5496-959a-a2ae7e6cf644" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}\pi " :db/id 17592186415962} {:answer/id #uuid "c8beac62-5cb9-5816-b59e-39200a1a65b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186415970} {:answer/id #uuid "cb82683b-e2da-594a-840f-2f2e47c75562" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186415971}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415962} :answer-field/id #uuid "33f085d7-1a2e-5ed1-949e-eab11615591e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415976}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ac50dc50-55cb-5157-8205-32f49dbad931" :question/math-academy-id "q-161338" :question/problem "![](images/fe/fe04241f55bae9dae231be6486a3c53985c8dc4af9e9656787267d9d852f829e.png)

$$

magnitude $\frac{1}{t+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$" :question/worked-solution "The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=3\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+1|=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2} \\  & =8{ln}^{2}⁡2-2{ln}^{2}⁡2 \\  & =6{ln}^{2}⁡(2)\,J.\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}7-\lambda  & -1 \\ 1 & 9-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(9-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot 1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-16\lambda +64 & =0 \\ (\lambda -8)(\lambda -8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=8.$

$$

"Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨-y,\,x⟩$ and the points $A(0,1)$ and $B(0,-1)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne 0,
$$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ in counterclockwise direction” is true. Parameterizing the curve, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}1\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi  \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,
$$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the segment line $\overset{―}{AB},$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$” is true. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨0,\,1-2t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨2t-1,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-2⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ is independent of path” is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ is path-dependent.

- Statement “$F$ is conservative” is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative."} {:db/id 17592186420352 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52a1dbcb-127d-567f-b362-0ca0b1d54e42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186420338} {:answer/id #uuid "748fa6b4-08c9-57b1-9c5f-ace131b66c19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186420342} {:answer/id #uuid "76cec32a-c27c-5e6c-94e2-bb27825747c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186420343} {:answer/id #uuid "b70ba875-07c9-5c3f-85df-154df641f91f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186420345} {:answer/id #uuid "ec20d6e5-b2d8-5e04-b68d-e1fd68f53231" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186420347}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420345} :answer-field/id #uuid "ff922856-e3c4-5b40-8d0e-cd85fae942ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420350}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "89fae1b5-1405-51b4-b87d-75b6acbbdc2e" :question/math-academy-id "q-82192" :question/problem "Find $7det(A)-2det(B)$, where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{3} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -0.5 & 2\end{bmatrix}.

Therefore, $7det(A)-2det(B)=7\cdot 0-2\cdot (-6)=12.$"} {:db/id 17592186420504 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f54eb3dc-8f1a-5dd1-962f-c6bca73b03cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186477271} {:answer/id #uuid "8c3bd524-ddd5-53ed-ac7b-67c5c3c6cc25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186477272}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477271} :answer-field/id #uuid "665a7adb-4995-5ab8-8dc0-620e006ab150" :answer-field/key "$H(1,1)>0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186477605} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "32a85eda-3d96-59fb-ae1a-38073082f1cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186477273} {:answer/id #uuid "dc13ebbc-79a8-5f41-b29b-888f990acc60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186477274}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477274} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e1f0653-0d7e-5971-b6ae-0758b0a5f1c6" :answer-field/key "$\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)>0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186477606} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e834f58-d2a9-5c2a-898e-e22835894832" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186477275} {:answer/id #uuid "793854ab-f508-5b37-924d-9eca03e5429b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186477276}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477275} :answer-field/id #uuid "56acc568-b4e3-5dd3-8613-65932ac1d099" :answer-field/key "The point $(1,1)$ is a local minimum of $f$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186477607}] :question/id #uuid "d1a7556c-36af-5f0b-b64c-a00089e6850e" :question/math-academy-id "q-37456" :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$ 
has the second derivative

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

and has a stationary point at $(1,1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement $H(1,1)>0$ is false. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(1,1),$ we get

$$
H(1,1)=det({f}^{″}(1,1))=2\cdot 0-{1}^{2}=-1<0.
$$

- Statement $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)>0$ is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)=({f}^{″}(1,1))_{11}=2>0.$

- Statement “The point $(1,1)$ is a local minimum of $f$” is false. Since $H(1,1)<0,$ then $(1,1)$ is a saddle point by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)>0$ only."} {:db/id 17592186420693 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "22fd7e43-5c76-592b-aee4-f521964cb28a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474690} {:answer/id #uuid "56db8c6a-3927-5f57-8d4a-f66704069758" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474691}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474690} :answer-field/id #uuid "5591e25a-3ea8-5f89-9be5-e954600bbcf0" :answer-field/key "$f$ is a differentiable function" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475271} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0aaacbae-01bd-5b78-b909-ba34f4a8bfe5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474692} {:answer/id #uuid "9df9fb08-bffb-50d9-9054-b845a6a759d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474693}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474692} :answer-field/id #uuid "a3b5576e-92d4-5f62-a180-abf1cc0efd81" :answer-field/key "$f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475272} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a32688b-9a6e-5531-97e4-13b963ffda66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474694} {:answer/id #uuid "65d2bf31-d717-50e7-9174-4e253ccf20e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474695}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474695} :answer-field/id #uuid "1bd972e0-15e5-5c38-b69b-4c566a479a6a" :answer-field/key "$f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C,$ for any $C\in R$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475273}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "390cc44c-87e5-5905-81de-8b4495a342fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-216459" :question/problem "$\,$ ${f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x$

Which of the following conditions are necessary and sufficient for the above statement to be true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Given that the equivalence $P⇔Q$ is true, we have that $P$ is a *necessary and sufficient condition* for $Q.$  

In our case, we need to find the conditions that are *necessary and sufficient* for the given one. In other words,

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇒\,\text{Condition}
$$

and

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇐\,\text{Condition}.
$$

Notice that the solution to the differential equation ${f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C\in R$ is the arbitrary constant.

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given conditions.

- Condition “$f$ is a differentiable function” is *not* a sufficient condition:

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇍\,(f\text{ is a differentiable function})\,\,\times 
$$

For example, the function $f(x)={e}^{x}$ is a differentiable function but ${f}^{′}(x)\ne {sec}^{2}⁡x.$

- Condition $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is *not* a necessary condition:

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇏\,(f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\,\times 
$$

For example, for the function $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1,$ the statement ${f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x$ is true but $f(x)\ne \operatorname{tan}⁡x+1.$

- Condition “$f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C,$ for any $C\in R$” is both necessary and sufficient: The statement ${f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x$ is true *if and only if* $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C,$ for any $C\in R.$

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇒\,(f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C)
$$

and

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇐\,(f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C).
$$

Therefore, we can write

$$
({f}^{′}(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x)\,⇔\,(f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C)\,\,✓
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C,$ for any $C\in R$” only."} {:db/id 17592186420847 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "336cb96e-8d35-5f9f-92e4-bf01f1fe608d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186420806} {:answer/id #uuid "5725181a-ff3e-5107-8722-cd79c0a511e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{14}" :db/id 17592186420811} {:answer/id #uuid "b75e75d9-4872-5fbc-a59d-3e54eebab508" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186420824} {:answer/id #uuid "bb525c0d-2a19-503f-b30d-3b12439ddf16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186420825} {:answer/id #uuid "cab0cf74-f931-5eb5-9974-e3db30298fa7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186420829}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420825} :answer-field/id #uuid "75968549-80b9-5200-918a-66a961c78ce2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420842}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0b58d794-d6a1-55fe-88d5-660b59bdd30a" :question/math-academy-id "q-42578" :question/problem "Find $det({A}^{-1}),$ if $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 6 & 5\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

Therefore, we obtain

det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186420848 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3dafe486-15fc-5abc-8a0d-2beb22386f42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186420809} {:answer/id #uuid "8e814c6a-3786-561d-9f46-38ef12a0585a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186420818} {:answer/id #uuid "90c1ce8c-7b18-5377-9a47-ace432f229bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186420819} {:answer/id #uuid "cc7cb828-c853-54d8-b205-d802c97b37f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186420830} {:answer/id #uuid "d2b62576-113c-5f4d-b29d-3ce30a3f8585" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186420831}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420819} :answer-field/id #uuid "660640e3-e8ef-509a-a758-3c65a1428537" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420841}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "37f105cd-9dd0-500b-bb29-7f9f80a1a14c" :question/math-academy-id "q-43071" :question/problem "Find $det({A}^{-1}),$ if $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

Therefore, we obtain

$$"} {:db/id 17592186420849 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "44a67a7f-7ce3-5fc4-9a99-c7b43778cf51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "77" :db/id 17592186420810} {:answer/id #uuid "755ff62c-e4b0-56e4-8933-fdd296936d8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-72" :db/id 17592186420815} {:answer/id #uuid "9577d942-a37d-5bb6-ad63-4cff94938a48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-42" :db/id 17592186420820} {:answer/id #uuid "b74bd5d3-d00b-534f-908c-090b06c3201d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-14" :db/id 17592186420823} {:answer/id #uuid "c498389f-d133-538a-bef9-88e693ebc92c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "76" :db/id 17592186420828}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420815} :answer-field/id #uuid "633fd2f4-984e-51bc-b51a-5f37a89e06b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "38d108f6-377b-5951-bc6b-4ec43d8b652b" :question/math-academy-id "q-88281" :question/problem "Given that $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix},
$$ find $det(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
det(A)=det\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that both matrices are triangular. Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(3\cdot (-1)\cdot 2)\cdot ((-1)\cdot 3\cdot (-4)) \\  & =(-6)\cdot 12 \\  & =-72.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186420850 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1de3d101-6ebd-5bbc-ad0b-5f1d9ed17bbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186420803} {:answer/id #uuid "3896dbb3-7bb1-5f7c-b8bf-88d4cf58a131" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186420808} {:answer/id #uuid "d2f0dcd3-6430-515f-8e85-02e0bf1c5fa4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186420832} {:answer/id #uuid "dd787881-42cf-53fe-9c3e-08b97bcc5ccf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186420834} {:answer/id #uuid "e50a27dc-031b-52dd-8815-f79824db9e9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186420837}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420803} :answer-field/id #uuid "db7de380-466f-5089-9f2e-e91927307109" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420846}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7f0a84be-936b-55f9-b169-54a768974c12" :question/math-academy-id "q-42577" :question/problem "Given that $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -7 & 1 & -3 \\ 6 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$ find $det(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
det(A)=det\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -7 & 1 & -3 \\ 6 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ -7 & 1 & -3 \\ 6 & 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}\cdot 1(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 6 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (8-6) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186420853 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15bb6772-ebfa-5300-9707-f0c44ba3ca38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{10}" :db/id 17592186420801} {:answer/id #uuid "1657176b-b7bb-5bac-8681-50357708185d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186420802} {:answer/id #uuid "341db512-89dd-5d60-9521-449fcc83f4d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186420807} {:answer/id #uuid "7ecdfc0d-790a-509f-8041-8c18f54a719a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186420817} {:answer/id #uuid "bd130b49-aec7-5947-9ffc-20dcb30a8a97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186420827}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420827} :answer-field/id #uuid "a81cf8c4-10bc-54bc-9308-65fe3b30e2ee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420844}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9e9ddda3-97aa-551d-9453-cae76713ec59" :question/math-academy-id "q-43070" :question/problem "Find $det({A}^{-1}),$ if $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}.
$$

First, we find $det(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =10-5 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=\frac{1}{5}.

$$

$$

$$

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C) & =\begin{vmatrix}6 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}4 & 0 & 5 \\ -6 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot (-1)(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(6-4)\cdot (-1)(12-5) \\  & =4\cdot (-7) \\  & =-28.\end{aligned}

from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The constant coefficient of the series is

$$
{a}_{0}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={cos}^{2}⁡(x)$ and $L=4,$ the constant coefficient becomes

$$
{a}_{0}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, the constant term of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=4$ and $f(x)={cos}^{2}⁡(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {\int }_{-4}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424003 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "31d5edd8-2b29-5eba-8a70-917a5b0f20f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{8}}" :db/id 17592186423969} {:answer/id #uuid "71609beb-d000-5d09-b83b-5c7ae828643f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}" :db/id 17592186423978} {:answer/id #uuid "a4655f58-d989-5a50-8b84-0a0259d6d8f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2{e}^{3}}" :db/id 17592186423984} {:answer/id #uuid "a59b312d-c446-5a83-97bf-18385fce9ef9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{9}}" :db/id 17592186423985} {:answer/id #uuid "bd231bf4-aff5-5dd1-9238-2dee00cd6f1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186423987}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423978} :answer-field/id #uuid "37078ec0-a9a2-5952-8060-4f2067bef6bb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423996}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "840fc6bd-43f7-5e1f-9678-e0daa00596e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-253929" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ calculate $P(X>6\,|\,X>4).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a random variable $X∼Exp(\lambda ),$ and two positive real numbers $s,t,$ the momeryless property of the exponential distribution states that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =2,$ $s=4,$ and $s+t=6.$ From this, we can find $t$ as follows:

$$
t=(t+s)-s=6-4=2
$$

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6\,|\,X>4) & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(2)\cdot (2)} \\  & ={e}^{-4} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424005 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00532a77-8369-5069-a645-da39692238cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-3{e}^{-2}" :db/id 17592186423964} {:answer/id #uuid "5ba4d575-3c96-585c-87ae-967c1404dc69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-2{e}^{-3}" :db/id 17592186423975} {:answer/id #uuid "6cf46d04-45a1-535e-a92e-c9cb35404ba7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{-2}" :db/id 17592186423976} {:answer/id #uuid "950530ce-1ae8-509e-b4cd-ed8ae399b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-6}" :db/id 17592186423981} {:answer/id #uuid "e23b4a6b-fba0-5d93-9ac6-0cd62b1a9f21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-{e}^{-6}" :db/id 17592186423990}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423990} :answer-field/id #uuid "e05b810e-c24f-55a7-bef2-0f820b29550d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423999}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b6017236-d9af-57fe-9a24-c8e569cb2642" :question/math-academy-id "q-253938" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ calculate $P(X\le 9\,|\,X>6).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a random variable $X∼Exp(\lambda ),$ and two positive real numbers $s,t,$ the memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =2,$ $s=6,$ and $s+t=9.$ From this, we can find $t$ as follows:

$$
t=(t+s)-s=9-6=3
$$

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 9\,|\,X>6) & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(2)\cdot (3)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "e80dcef6-8cf3-58d4-8627-98be0f13b772" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,{sec}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424272} {:db/id 17592186424279 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6ebb2cb7-894c-5ea1-8fe9-5d932e0eaec2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424266} {:answer/id #uuid "bc944f96-6c8b-5c8c-9ec9-40c54f081a5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424267} {:answer/id #uuid "c290b836-3e40-5e91-84ff-1cbd84d8ae28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424269} {:answer/id #uuid "e80dcef6-8cf3-58d4-8627-98be0f13b772" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,{sec}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424272} {:answer/id #uuid "ead5149a-8ad0-50cd-aebf-6ea20a3a902d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424273}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424273} :answer-field/id #uuid "6da65985-bad5-5a30-9563-e72ed071e141" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424277}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "82f90d91-406e-5d3c-bce9-9c8235648ab0" :question/math-academy-id "q-138851" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}.$ Its derivative is given by

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(2x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))+(2x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2(\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$"} {:answer/id #uuid "055b0e6b-d664-5538-b782-3dfbe82f8ee7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} $P(X\le \frac{5}{6}\,|\,X>\frac{2}{3}).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a random variable $X∼Exp(\lambda ),$ and two positive real numbers $s,t,$ the memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =3,$ $s=\frac{2}{3},$ and $s+t=\frac{5}{6}.$ From this, we can find $t$ as follows:

$$
t=(t+s)-s=\frac{5}{6}-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{6}
$$

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le \frac{5}{6}\,|\,X>\frac{2}{3}) & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(3)\cdot (1/6)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424578 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25fb97a5-9ed6-5c98-8031-485552414117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-5{e}^{-3/5}" :db/id 17592186424531} {:answer/id #uuid "4cbd30f8-0317-54c7-8a80-7f23503ecca6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-3}" :db/id 17592186424542} {:answer/id #uuid "5151c7de-e2f6-5856-b422-07c5dab2d5f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-{e}^{-3}" :db/id 17592186424543} {:answer/id #uuid "e5bcecd5-8331-5e54-9822-a05d7243d9b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{-1/5}" :db/id 17592186424560} {:answer/id #uuid "f5b3ce16-7f1a-5313-be26-0788d6b661a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-{e}^{-1/5}" :db/id 17592186424564}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424543} :answer-field/id #uuid "3a0a548f-8bd4-50d5-8207-5dc86f15188f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424569}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a86905dc-6d69-50e5-afb3-4d8bb353dbfd" :question/math-academy-id "q-253936" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right),$ calculate $P(X\le 9\,|\,X>4).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a random variable $X∼Exp(\lambda ),$ and two positive real numbers $s,t,$ the memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{3}{5},$ $s=4,$ and $s+t=9.$ From this, we can find $t$ as follows:

$$
t=(t+s)-s=9-4=5
$$

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 9\,|\,X>4) & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(3/5)\cdot (5)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424899 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "171230a8-065f-5312-91ff-166c6fb3df4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}" :db/id 17592186424893} {:answer/id #uuid "21bc26a0-57ad-5e62-a6e6-621e2ba24583" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}" :db/id 17592186424894} {:answer/id #uuid "54d72f80-7a7b-5b93-a0ec-2d6edad08ac4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186424895} {:answer/id #uuid "6c11e90f-184e-57bd-b3ed-1971d8fb82ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}:=-{R}_{2}" :db/id 17592186424896} {:answer/id #uuid "acde6755-f2db-5c6c-bdc1-ac03bdaa2931" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186424897}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424894} :answer-field/id #uuid "c75bea69-7db0-5820-97b1-b5dd95b8b845" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424898}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "200dace6-387b-586f-87ab-a5501c01cbe0" :question/math-academy-id "q-130851" :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 5\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 5\end{vmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}.

x∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{{field-4}}\cdot {{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ bounded by the polar circles $r=2$ and $r=3,$ as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to its distance from the origin. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=kr,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{3}kr\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{3}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{2}^{3}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}\,{|}_{2}^{3}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =k\cdot \frac{19}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{38\pi k}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=kr=\frac{3M}{38\pi }r.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{38\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{3}r\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{38\pi }({\int }_{2}^{3}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{38\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\,{|}_{2}^{3}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3M}{38\pi }\cdot \frac{211}{5}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{633M}{95}.\end{aligned}

Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=k{r}^{2},$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}k{r}^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =k\cdot 2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi k.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=k{r}^{2}=\frac{M}{\pi }{r}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{M}{\pi }\cdot \frac{13}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{13M}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426165 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ae42d1a-6d46-5f68-a58f-63f3f01ba083" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "M" :db/id 17592186426083} {:answer/id #uuid "84a648d6-9b98-5e2b-96c3-2d8410a9822a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M" :db/id 17592186426114} {:answer/id #uuid "8e598212-d811-50b7-bec5-2b0589d8de38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{2}" :db/id 17592186426118} {:answer/id #uuid "b95793fa-2522-5d8c-bf1a-4e74f2539faf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4M" :db/id 17592186426132} {:answer/id #uuid "dd025262-3d7b-5e61-b549-0d29e583e1df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{4}" :db/id 17592186426138}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426118} :answer-field/id #uuid "9936f427-3e8b-5ed5-aa88-8837211a03b0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426156}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6773c2a6-0930-567e-b7b2-ce599d9b40d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163244" :question/problem "![](images/cc/ccf2ad2b3d8b39dbacdcdce6bd317c5720ce3b750249f6c328e60d3c74ddb4ef.png)

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

First, notice that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

The area of the plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.

$$"} {:db/id 17592186426267 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "df195bef-be90-5b17-81c7-6ebe22d082fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x" :db/id 17592186426255}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426255} :answer-field/id #uuid "05bbd010-f6f1-5bf4-b78d-793dba0e386e" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186426260} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58a8df56-e805-5459-8255-ce8d0ce32e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186426246}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426246} :answer-field/id #uuid "167f892e-c054-5442-a4a4-6b111df78980" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186426261} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8043153a-4007-5470-98ef-3dcb581ee71e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-x" :db/id 17592186426247}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426247} :answer-field/id #uuid "b327a6ea-c521-5ff3-9905-1a3b91e728ad" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186426264}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "317b9d0c-4dca-5b66-9042-f920e2ca78b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-275499" :question/problem "A stick of length $1$ is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In this problem, the break point $X$ is uniformly distributed over the interval $[0,1]$, so the probability density function is

$$
f(x)=1,\,0\le x\le 1.
$$

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $1-X.$ The longer of the two pieces, $Y,$ is therefore given by

$$
Y=max(X,1-X).
$$

Therefore, we define

$$
r(x)=max(x,1-x).
$$

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

- if $0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}$, then $x\le 1-x$, so the longer piece has length $1-x,$

- if $\frac{1}{2}<x\le 1$, then $x>1-x$, so the longer piece has length $x.$

Therefore,

$$
r(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}1-x, & \,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}, \\ x, & \,\frac{1}{2}<x\le 1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[max(X,1-X)] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}(1-x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1/2}^{1}x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}(1-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1/2}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/2}+{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2})+(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8})+(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{3}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected length of the longer piece is $\frac{3}{4}.$"} {:db/id 17592186426269 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05928321-6f6f-5ce5-acf1-3dd017571004" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25}{8}" :db/id 17592186426236} {:answer/id #uuid "140bcf46-7a00-52f5-b945-23c1c8dfa78d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13}{8}" :db/id 17592186426237} {:answer/id #uuid "4504b779-0714-5211-bbac-0fed711fc93e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}" :db/id 17592186426241} {:answer/id #uuid "babd2cda-6b21-57ae-be62-698db9e28b8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{8}" :db/id 17592186426252} {:answer/id #uuid "d56a8ba0-3ef7-5ef2-9dfb-d113fd51667f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{23}{8}" :db/id 17592186426254}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426241} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce3eb618-d116-5818-bdb6-673400ec83db" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426266}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a62d513-53a5-5f10-88b4-24713c5a800b" :question/math-academy-id "q-136884" :question/problem "A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. Find $\text{E}[{log}_{2}⁡(X)].$

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ |" :question/worked-solution "For a discrete random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\sum }_{x\in S}r(x)f(x).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
r(x)={log}_{2}⁡x.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{log}_{2}⁡(X)] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\,f(x) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(2)\cdot \frac{1}{8}+{log}_{2}⁡(4)\cdot \frac{1}{2}+{log}_{2}⁡(8)\cdot \frac{3}{8} \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{8}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+3\cdot \frac{3}{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}+1+\frac{9}{8} \\  & =\frac{18}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426308 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "332694ea-bd99-5523-b1d8-48a224b3dc34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186426297} {:answer/id #uuid "6ed8db16-e8bd-5c83-b560-aef74fb47014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186426299} {:answer/id #uuid "864823ca-9fd6-5647-872e-3574bd6be0c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186426300} {:answer/id #uuid "d90a60bf-c9df-5642-a65f-043b1fbac549" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186426303} {:answer/id #uuid "f712f3e2-029b-5a8a-b19e-340bb36a3186" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186426304}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426300} :answer-field/id #uuid "7ea44ec1-58ba-5956-a980-aec4c772ced8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "60094f6c-d2bd-58df-8627-15176f255263" :question/math-academy-id "q-104435" :question/problem "The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$
equals $2.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}k & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2 & k \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-k-6)-0+1(6-k) \\  & =-k-6+6-k \\  & =-2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{12} & =(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-2-2) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{21}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2k}\cdot 4 \\  & =-\frac{2}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{21}^{′}=2$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{k} & =2 \\ -2 & =2k \\ -\frac{2}{2} & =k \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426309 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16cc7665-faef-5318-96fb-c89a1b7adc64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -8 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186426296} {:answer/id #uuid "39a3852a-5680-51e4-9e2a-405e8aa0a909" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -8 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186426298} {:answer/id #uuid "95310ad0-4ea0-549a-b41e-47e2e1481ffb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 8 & -3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186426301} {:answer/id #uuid "b9fbec83-d0b7-55ad-a7b0-15c8c1d2d21d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -8 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186426302} {:answer/id #uuid "fc2f21f0-c001-5a27-883c-872065513e5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 8 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186426305}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426298} :answer-field/id #uuid "4b1f25d6-5390-5fe3-998f-b7a40d9649c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426306}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ccf4f432-0d42-54bc-b36a-bd39fd754033" :question/math-academy-id "q-73478" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
given that $det(A)=-3.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** We are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 8 & -3 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ -8 & -3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -8 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -8 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.

{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky-3sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=-\frac{15}{2}sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-\frac{15}{2}sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t),$ which is $\frac{5}{2},$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)}^{2}=\frac{5}{2}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186427273 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26077737-8ba6-52d8-a130-7bb98621fc19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186427249} {:answer/id #uuid "34b4e83a-d0e0-527d-a53e-c34aa3793a56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186427250} {:answer/id #uuid "4f792fe5-ab17-5321-a1fb-b45187d74bee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186427254} {:answer/id #uuid "a2163383-f83a-5102-8354-9dd07eb8238d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186427260} {:answer/id #uuid "b5a30bf1-16e7-552c-abd3-762c6873fb4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186427261}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427250} :answer-field/id #uuid "be790569-47e5-5c68-b35d-041a395703da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427269}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ae78c4ab-202a-5311-a7a5-9b6c9263c259" :question/math-academy-id "q-94237" :question/problem "The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

{{field-2}} $,\,$

$$
a=\begin{bmatrix}-7 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,c=\begin{bmatrix}13 \\ 11 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,d=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 5 & 13 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. So, we have

$$
det(M)=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 5 & 13 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=(-7)\cdot (-2)\cdot (-5)\cdot 1=-70.
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|-70|=70.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "5e5262af-da0e-5a59-8704-7c9dacf4de2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{2}-\operatorname{tan}⁡x+K" :db/id 17592186429914} {:db/id 17592186429930 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5e5262af-da0e-5a59-8704-7c9dacf4de2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{2}-\operatorname{tan}⁡x+K" :db/id 17592186429914} {:answer/id #uuid "9f63075a-1c8a-5a7b-92d3-a38ee960a89e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+K" :db/id 17592186429916} {:answer/id #uuid "9fd0f034-ce27-5ace-8026-4eaf6cb1ce68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+K" :db/id 17592186429917} {:answer/id #uuid "f18bdd3d-8085-5e2e-822e-62d75b040c5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x|+K" :db/id 17592186429923} {:answer/id #uuid "f602ed78-2e15-5cdc-81a3-3dc36a33f074" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x|+K" :db/id 17592186429925}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186429916} :answer-field/id #uuid "5edcce3e-e53a-5f19-ab28-fc88ce15b3a5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186429926}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "305ab7d8-b9f8-5861-8b01-dd9a503b80df" :question/math-academy-id "q-113997" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}(u-1)\text{d}u \\  & =\int (1-\frac{1}{u})\,\text{d}u \\  & =u-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+K\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=C+1.$"} {:db/id 17592186429931 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bde6a22f-af92-5d05-a00e-ee43025b38b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186429918}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186429918} :answer-field/id #uuid "e4b1c21c-bb6c-5c53-b4e6-f6635e6c2be4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186429928}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "66f3c3b9-c1e9-58f7-9604-16a02027760f" :question/math-academy-id "q-355818" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. "5eff5095-a0c0-5448-9e3d-e45ec11b1792" :question/math-academy-id "q-109186" :question/problem "![](images/a7/a70a12201e99ded8eed85b797c760862814e1f0a50129020fa6d3b35d4334394.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts (see figure above). What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm n\pi ,\,n\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186430448 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b6147f2-99cb-5e0e-bfe7-1ab9fcb4bfaf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186430425} {:answer/id #uuid "3bd5f2d0-f063-5f9a-8554-0e38b366ddee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186430426} {:answer/id #uuid "4c3b39c3-ebcc-501e-bf32-f62c8ab6fbca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186430428} {:answer/id #uuid "9f8b4808-0307-5f43-b835-eaa5d7c78ac1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186430432} {:answer/id #uuid "e1d3bd0b-8f50-5fda-8e7a-df552a252f05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186430436}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186430425} :answer-field/id #uuid "57597420-75c9-5305-b6c7-82cc31ede092" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186430440}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f2460b1b-0ae3-5791-81e8-e644fac55aa1" :question/math-academy-id "q-102692" :question/problem "Given that 
$$
\displaystyle {f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} & 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},
$$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
$$
\displaystyle {f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} & 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},
$$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\right)=-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\right)=\frac{2y}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{2y}{x} & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=(-1)\cdot 0-2\cdot 2=-4.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "37e9bbb5-54b5-5e26-a0a0-50d7cf20ec9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{25}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9231aa24-53fe-5011-80b7-3b4b62ca8c09" :question/math-academy-id "q-83966" :question/problem "Evaluate

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-{1}^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{4}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{5\pi /3}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(-\frac{4}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡(2\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ))-(-\frac{4}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{3}\right))] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(-\frac{4}{3}+1)-(-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186430774 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37e9bbb5-54b5-5e26-a0a0-50d7cf20ec9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{25}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186430735} {:answer/id #uuid "6ef3239f-a18f-5059-bc4c-90c9f800c498" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{5}{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186430746} {:answer/id #uuid "eb9c6068-17a0-54f3-9151-2a048c9f0abc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{5}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186430759} {:answer/id #uuid "f3db7076-912a-5dca-b78b-50d779ed3d9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{5}{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186430761} {:answer/id #uuid "f55622cc-0b32-52f4-8ae8-9cf843cdb023" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{25}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186430762}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186430759} :answer-field/id #uuid "e75c2f8e-ad0e-567f-ad60-4f9161bdb2d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186430767}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b93ec44e-b9fb-53f6-875f-5ef36dc8b48a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161043" :question/problem "![](images/2d/2db1e29e5f911a45c4c48ab41c4ad6dc63eeb36a8112672ae66844e14342f4c0.png)

$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}({tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that ${tan}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{3}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-{sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186431112 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ade44e9-b6f9-500e-bc09-791aec3c4112" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186431063} {:answer/id #uuid "6590c99b-1fe0-54a5-9f86-8aebcedc658b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186431071} {:answer/id #uuid "6d4d7986-64b5-5587-b804-bab2a0930585" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186431072} {:answer/id #uuid "ae2dad62-d368-5197-b93b-e3e45fe17653" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186431081} {:answer/id #uuid "fd953cc5-abf5-5b0c-84f3-3e4672a326d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{3}" :db/id 17592186431097}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186431071} :answer-field/id #uuid "e803221b-b806-5450-a5a1-2379c91d357f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186431108}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "49b73c78-3335-57b5-a631-c7f8dd771090" :question/math-academy-id "q-73365" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we use the fact that $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}(1-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\left(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)-\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186431113 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e1161462-0f9d-545a-a5a5-27e6a35427ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1" :db/id 17592186431092}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186431092} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fe9e96d-c290-5de0-aea5-06fc2a18c7e7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186431102}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "77e54e57-de69-5688-a9c9-dfe71c2ce5e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-352711" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. $$

$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the identities $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $$
\displaystyle \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,
$$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186431116 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05f4f35f-6fb8-5362-bb51-1c0b0c319dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}" :db/id 17592186431055} {:answer/id #uuid "14b36ff5-eeb9-52d4-b7b8-21c79368f8b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{26\sqrt{3}}{27}" :db/id 17592186431056} {:answer/id #uuid "41aaf43b-2c95-50cf-a8a3-79ae4c22104b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\sqrt{3}}{20}" :db/id 17592186431064} {:answer/id #uuid "85271a33-9aae-5b9d-a3b8-a96dd470bdac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14\sqrt{3}}{27}" :db/id 17592186431074} {:answer/id #uuid "dcaf3e71-8a60-5d8e-be80-97ff5b0a7a92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}" :db/id 17592186431091}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186431056} :answer-field/id #uuid "82084fd2-bb79-5568-8b5b-a9fbb9530769" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186431103}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c26cdc41-d401-5858-96e0-ffa4a20294ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-49279" :question/problem "$$
