$$" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,du={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/3}^{\sqrt{3}}{u}^{2}\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}{|}_{\sqrt{3}/3}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({(\sqrt{3})}^{3}-{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(3-\frac{1}{9}) \\  & =\frac{26\sqrt{3}}{27}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186431117 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4783ae01-0409-5f42-a49a-a5011eafe80c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}" :db/id 17592186431065}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186431065} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cb6fe3-1966-59eb-9541-67fe64eb26b5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186431106}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "cdc94a5e-ffa3-5e3c-b067-8b7e71e5c799" :question/math-academy-id "q-358219" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}3\operatorname{sec}⁡2x{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(sin\,\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)-sin\,(0)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186431118 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "86a74f3d-6597-59e4-b81c-8406532b8b29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{3}-3" :db/id 17592186431076}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186431076} :answer-field/id #uuid "0a251513-9691-50f6-b973-f2685262f1ed" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186431100}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d54d59da-aeb4-5592-b790-f9a9feee5b10" :question/math-academy-id "q-358220" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}\frac{9}{{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x=
$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡3x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}\frac{9}{{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}9{\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}\right)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}9{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /9}{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=3x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=3x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{9}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,k \\  & =-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+0\cdot 0 \\  & =2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi (2-0) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}

The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$

Recall the following:

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =\begin{vmatrix}2{sin}^{2}⁡x & 1-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\ {(2{sin}^{2}⁡x)}^{′} & {(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)}^{′}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2{sin}^{2}⁡x & 1-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2{sin}^{2}⁡x)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-4({sin}^{2}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

which is $\text{zero for all }x\in R.$

:question/math-academy-id "q-163781" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈5+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=-3$ and $det(A)=8$” is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-3$ and

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -3\end{vmatrix}=8.
$$

- Statement “$A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite” is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-3<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -3\end{vmatrix}=8>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is negative-definite.

- Statement “$a$ is a local maximum of $f$” is true. Since the matrix $A$ is negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “${a}_{11}=-3$ and $det(A)=8$”; “$a$ is a local maximum of $f$” only."} {:db/id 17592186434755 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=2$ and $det(A)=3$” is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=2$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(2)-1(1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite” is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=2>0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}=2>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=3>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is positive-definite.

- Statement “$a$ is a saddle point of $f$” is false. Since the matrix $A$ is positive-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local minimum of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “${a}_{11}=2$ and $det(A)=3$” only."} {:db/id 17592186434759 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a7ce264d-034d-56ae-8c45-60644fea8382" - if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=-1$ and $det(A)=-15$” is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-1,$ but

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}-4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1(3)-4(4)+2(-6) \\  & =-31.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$A$ is negative-definite” is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-1<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{vmatrix}=-19<0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-31<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement “$a$ is a local minimum of $f$” is false. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186434981 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39640287-9487-5ac3-85d7-aedbf5d97773" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-4,-4)$" :db/id 17592186434956} {:answer/id #uuid "3c018145-70ed-5572-bd19-1c77a5f9feed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(-4,-4)$" :db/id 17592186434957} {:answer/id #uuid "c1c03577-b7e1-599b-a3bf-f0b6d8f8b9b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(-4,-4)$" :db/id 17592186434965} {:answer/id #uuid "c5596b05-f02f-56da-a832-f2b3413b0aa5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434967} {:answer/id #uuid "ffb56293-94a9-5eda-9354-4caedfa03d63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434976}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186434956} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf6f62c2-36fa-58b4-83fb-e251b870cb3c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186434980}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "05076731-f2b5-5426-b032-1f0962af8ee1" :question/math-academy-id "q-105278" :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)=xy-4x-4y-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ and determine which of the following statements is true." :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-4x-4y-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-4x-4y-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y-4-2x & x-4-2y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y-4-2x &=0 \\ x-4-2y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
y-4-2x=0\,⟹\,y=2x+4
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4-2(2x+4) & =0 \\ -3x-12 & =0 \\ x & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=2x+4,$ we obtain

$$
x=-4\,⟹\,y=2(-4)+4=-4.
$$

Hence, $(-4,-4)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4-2x)=-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-4-2y)=1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4-2)=1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-4-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-4,-4),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-4,-4)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-4,-4),$ we get

$$
H(-4,-4)=det({f}^{″}(-4,-4))=(-2)^{2}-{1}^{2}=3>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-4,-4)=({f}^{″}(-4,-4))_{11}=-2<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-4,-4).$"} {:db/id 17592186434982 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c27e9b4e-206f-5150-a881-d37dde9c4e85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(3,1)$ and a local maximum $(-3,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434966} {:answer/id #uuid "d2284ea7-6bfd-52fc-b08e-cbc5dc03d189" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-3,1)$ and a local minimum $(-3,1)$" :db/id 17592186434969} {:answer/id #uuid "e02c6dc0-e019-5937-b18e-930a68cb954f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(3,1)$ and a local maximum $(-3,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434971} {:answer/id #uuid "e957c6c0-0532-521e-b2c3-2747f7ac1033" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(-3,1)$ and a saddle point at $(-3,1)$" :db/id 17592186434972} {:answer/id #uuid "f5d5c20b-2412-5e45-a4e7-034876616c97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186434975} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce8b2aa5-8481-5045-bb5b-59aa8a2d0aa3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186434979}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0a336a18-c506-59a2-baef-25499733a8d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-81179" :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(xy-3)\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}xy-3 &=0 \\ {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
xy-3=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{x}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9{\left(\frac{3}{x}\right)}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}-81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-81 & =0 \\ x & =-3,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{3}{x},$ we obtain

$$
x=-3\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{-3}=-1,\,\,x=3\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{3}=1.
$$

Hence, $(-3,-1)$ and $(3,1)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-6)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-6)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=-18y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -18y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 6 & -18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(3,1),$ we get

$$
H(3,1)=det({f}^{″}(3,1))=2\cdot (-18)-{6}^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(3,1)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-3,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-3,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -6 \\ -6 & 18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-3,-1),$ we get

$$
H(-3,-1)=det({f}^{″}(-3,-1))=(-2)\cdot 18-(-6)^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(-3,-1)$ is a saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1).$"} {:db/id 17592186434983 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b99dcd31-0696-5ae3-a002-0700a699c3c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453886} {:answer/id #uuid "b13cab50-ce9f-50ad-b0dc-b0f33b90172e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453887}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453887} :answer-field/id #uuid "aa4b6b9c-5d2a-594c-960e-1c4e75c64792" :answer-field/key "$H(-1,0)>0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454693} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6df70a2f-70bb-5fcc-ae8d-49c71465bbc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453888} {:answer/id #uuid "eeb49d3c-662c-5e17-871f-5d0e954249ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453889}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453889} :answer-field/id #uuid "abbc8d9a-f48f-5dd7-ab15-6b078f09b474" :answer-field/key "$\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,0)>0$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454694} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25f80279-e5d1-50e6-9fc4-c16efd13157c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453890} {:answer/id #uuid "b82e04f0-14eb-531c-b7af-055ded9e9fa6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453891}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453890} :answer-field/id #uuid "fdec8465-2901-52b6-a16f-9134ee75d3b0" :answer-field/key "The point $(-1,0)$ is a local maximum of $f$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454695}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b007310c-a11f-531c-b695-1febe8ef0462" :question/math-academy-id "q-37589" :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$ 
has the second derivative

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}12{x}^{2}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

and has a stationary point at $(-1,0).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,0),$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,0)=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement $H(-1,0)>0$ is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,0),$ we get

$$
H(-1,0)=det({f}^{″}(-1,0))=8\cdot 2-{0}^{2}=16>0.
$$

- Statement $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,0)>0$ is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,0)=({f}^{″}(-1,0))_{11}=8>0.$

- Statement “The point $(-1,0)$ is a local maximum of $f$” is false. Since $H(-1,0)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,0)>0,$ the point $(-1,0)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is $H(-1,0)>0$; $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,0)>0$ only."} {:answer/id #uuid "c63274df-6f1f-56f7-bcf0-d35e3a9b440e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{4}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186435110} {:db/id 17592186435123 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "217edb44-0fc7-5d6d-964e-6c05dca7cb50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡2{\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{3{t}^{2}+{2}^{t}}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186435095} {:answer/id #uuid "53eb5f8d-2c90-56b2-af3c-af00df5e8365" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{3}\sqrt{3{t}^{2}+{2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186435100} {:answer/id #uuid "97765c6f-bd17-5d3b-a5c6-230f3b86329e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡2{\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186435107} {:answer/id #uuid "aa6427b7-b0e6-5e33-9aca-612cfab836af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{3t}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186435108} {:answer/id #uuid "c63274df-6f1f-56f7-bcf0-d35e3a9b440e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{4}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186435110}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435110} :answer-field/id #uuid "a5dd24f4-4688-5465-a47d-3059c114e3fd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435120}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "048f2885-159c-5d24-83a6-9ee301309f6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-139070" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{3},\,y={2}^{t},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t})={2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{({2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{2}^{2t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{2}^{t}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+{4}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435128 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c3ac195-5a28-5c11-99ed-a06a6384cb26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{12\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186435091} {:answer/id #uuid "206381c1-a55a-5bbf-8129-7ade3cea9753" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{64\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186435094} {:answer/id #uuid "333420d8-3841-5986-a880-12239e3b0c86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186435098} {:answer/id #uuid "867968e5-1470-5d6b-bbb2-c22bb39822ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{45\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186435104} {:answer/id #uuid "8f4dc2f2-4b7b-5c53-9837-433249177feb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{32\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186435105}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435105} :answer-field/id #uuid "f67f1dc2-47fa-5fa4-a382-f69736f1f021" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435121}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d124471f-78aa-50f9-bfd3-0eadf2ea5bb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-138972" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $$
\displaystyle \frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}={sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right),
$$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\cdot |2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)|\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right))\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right).$ Then, $$
\displaystyle \text{d}u=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\,\text{d}t.
$$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right))\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{0}-2(1-{u}^{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1-{u}^{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi \cdot {[u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =16\pi (1-\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =16\pi \left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{32\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435147 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "039d5f33-dfa0-51c2-93be-2b7000137d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186435129} {:answer/id #uuid "0597b830-4974-5289-8d3c-e5ddb2d894f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186435130} {:answer/id #uuid "274c794a-3cbb-5dc2-bbb2-1f1131f70f1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186435131} {:answer/id #uuid "28126022-8f20-5f62-8417-0685db76f23b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186435132} {:answer/id #uuid "3b9511ec-b4f9-5c7b-b596-beebd0bcb054" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186435134}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435132} :answer-field/id #uuid "d554649a-905d-57c6-af27-cc40c4c45a3a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435146}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "0807a9e2-ba3b-5d6e-8562-a580bc61f62a" :question/math-academy-id "q-104515" :question/problem "Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-z &=5+3y \\ 3z-2y &=6-x\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-3y-z &=5 \\ x-2y+3z &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-9-2)-(9+1)-2(-6+3) \\  & =-22-10+6 \\  & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 10 & -3 \\ -1 & 8 & -5 \\ -7 & 4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & -10 & -3 \\ 1 & 8 & 5 \\ -7 & -4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-26 \\ 26 \\ -26\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=1-1+1=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186435395 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "012e8862-6d84-5ca3-808d-e580b5b68412" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186435375} {:answer/id #uuid "1d97894b-06e8-5458-afce-3b6280583bcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186435377} {:answer/id #uuid "49af7f88-d313-53b2-a836-26eef4f823e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186435381} {:answer/id #uuid "6341ade3-f46e-594c-b2db-483df7d6f5cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186435383} {:answer/id #uuid "e9393f5b-f485-5c2a-b52d-4ac15221029b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186435387}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435375} :answer-field/id #uuid "835cf471-5984-50ad-ac7a-5c92395f40c6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435392}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e525b492-a29a-585f-8c96-2055a51f2341" :question/math-academy-id "q-102686" :question/problem "Given that 
$$
\displaystyle {f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2} & 2y{x}^{2}-1\end{bmatrix},
$$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2} & 2y{x}^{2}-1\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}-1.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2}-1)=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2}-1)=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=2\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-12.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435474 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b1c5124-6786-5d81-9669-feb36452def2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{\pi }" :db/id 17592186435418} {:answer/id #uuid "38c37042-86a8-5705-8958-ac0d4b1fd085" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{2\pi }{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}" :db/id 17592186435424} {:answer/id #uuid "6e99f6b6-bdea-51a0-a2eb-7caa09bac7ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{3}}" :db/id 17592186435433} {:answer/id #uuid "6fcd075f-f1a4-5942-b9ec-bf178e03c53e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3\pi }}" :db/id 17592186435434} {:answer/id #uuid "fbba27fb-ffce-5ef2-8b79-e4a092ae27ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}" :db/id 17592186435458}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435458} :answer-field/id #uuid "d338a349-3b9f-5d71-b3f4-8e6e22455c77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435466}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bf2295d7-f3f0-5779-bd98-5a2f23825eae" :question/math-academy-id "q-163592" :question/problem "![](images/c0/c018d9df9a75b6c124b1e49b9c2359a0f8c70a5322d7ce9c04e05722005e8e8e.png)

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in  bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2,$ and the lines $y=x,$ $y=-x$ in the first and fourth quadrant, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,\,-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $$
\displaystyle \lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{ln}⁡2}.
$$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \theta {|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{M}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi M}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi M}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435719 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bebf495e-8b3b-5a9d-a588-759127f24c06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{8}" :db/id 17592186435704}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435704} :answer-field/id #uuid "dff647f1-983f-5ba6-9928-87a2fdcf179e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186435714}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e7130a2f-a2af-518c-8ac7-89bf1a4dc82f" :question/math-academy-id "q-343673" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky-4sin\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=-8sin\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-8sin\,(\frac{3}{2}t),$ which is $\frac{3}{2},$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}=\frac{9}{8}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "0697a92c-8206-5e12-8a38-d0cce8f0b796" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+5{cot}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436396} {:answer/id #uuid "2396ae55-dd62-5c4f-8d14-716f3b077ffd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-5{cot}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436400} {:db/id 17592186436436 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0697a92c-8206-5e12-8a38-d0cce8f0b796" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+5{cot}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436396} {:answer/id #uuid "0ad53142-ca5c-5050-8255-c2bf7f34c973" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-5\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436397} {:answer/id #uuid "2396ae55-dd62-5c4f-8d14-716f3b077ffd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-5{cot}^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436400} {:answer/id #uuid "7a0f1722-492f-5d0d-b85d-b801f734974d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-5\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436408} {:answer/id #uuid "f7191b76-8b73-524d-9752-f1a9544d8d3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+5\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186436424}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436397} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e7afbe3-da6c-5c70-9675-1af28ae108a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436428}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2ab531ef-b57e-5769-8250-354ac0b4cc1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-73517" :question/problem "$$

$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the Pythagorean identity:

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{7}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡x+x+2{cos}^{2}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{2}^{7}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+2({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{2}^{7}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+2\cdot 1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{2}^{7}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x+2}\,{|}_{2}^{7} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{7+2}-\sqrt{2+2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436439 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b4fbc1c-3545-5745-89f4-848a4e77fc0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{6})+C" :db/id 17592186436398} {:answer/id #uuid "6779cc08-804c-549e-a688-72a8c218ac7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{6})+C" :db/id 17592186436405} {:answer/id #uuid "70b508c8-5bef-5ba4-be2d-d5c002a6fd14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{6})+C" :db/id 17592186436407} {:answer/id #uuid "949785f1-bc84-54a6-aa50-79802f8ac400" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{6})+C" :db/id 17592186436414} {:answer/id #uuid "b96b832a-78b1-56de-b64f-6e8bbc3e0065" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{6})+C" :db/id 17592186436419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436419} :answer-field/id #uuid "fde1e6aa-3904-5bc7-8bc1-4efe5c7c9097" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436435}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4a652b8e-bfd2-5735-84e4-910c649c4ba7" :question/math-academy-id "q-49323" :question/problem "Calculate $$

$$" :question/worked-solution "From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =x-\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

Substituting the above into our integral gives

Do not round the answer.

$$

$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,1-{cos}^{2}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$

$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)={cos}^{2}⁡x,$ $a=0,$ and $b=\pi .$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-10)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}+10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-10)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "01f00612-ca24-58a9-9a99-5bc9dff70695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{sin}^{3}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t" :db/id 17592186442225} {:answer/id #uuid \displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{y{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{y{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}[\operatorname{tan}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi /4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{tan}⁡0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442609 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186442594}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442594} :answer-field/id #uuid "11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186442601}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7043d5b3-b126-54ab-a0bc-9816029b7532" :question/math-academy-id "q-223120" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$, find the principal normal vector $N(t)$ at an arbitrary point on the curve.

$N(t)=$
$⟨\,0\,,$
{{field-1}}
$\,,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the unit tangent vector $T(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡2t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\  & =-2⟨0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =|-2|\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{cos}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{-2⟨0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩}{2} \\  & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442614 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "85f9b3c0-76af-5d80-92a4-5941254da04b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sin t" :db/id 17592186442583}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442583} :answer-field/id #uuid "9f8052c5-663c-518b-bb07-10ee30f768f0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186442606}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f357a402-4ed9-5871-9002-ee2ada823334" :question/math-academy-id "q-358780" :question/problem "$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{13}(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+12\,k).
$$

The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given above. Find the principal normal vector to that curve at an arbitrary point on the curve.

$i\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{13}(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+12\,k)) \\  & =\frac{1}{13}(-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12)\,k) \\  & =\frac{5}{13}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{5}{13}‖\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j‖ \\  & =\frac{5}{13}\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{13}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{5}{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{13}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)}{\frac{5}{13}} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443229 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2d85bffd-8755-5e9b-a7b3-89febd886899" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186443106} {:answer/id #uuid "36fa518b-6582-5224-a8cb-c3138d904c19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186443108} {:answer/id #uuid "78fccd02-9cc5-55f5-b63f-230bd2ea38ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186443145} {:answer/id #uuid "d25d6992-22c7-51c6-8f7a-dcf497256df6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186443181} {:answer/id #uuid "fb6df07a-d7ae-549b-8810-208c22275136" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186443202}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186443181} :answer-field/id #uuid "a944373a-a6f7-5cc7-b56a-d45f56447bab" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186443216}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1812d74c-f7ff-5b92-ad0c-d300745fe3f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-334643" :question/problem "A numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $Δx=0.09,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.09)=0.20.$

- With step size $Δx=0.06,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.06)=0.05.$

Estimate the order of the numerical method." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.09$ to $0.06.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.09}{0.06}=1.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}=(1.5)^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.20$ to $0.05.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.20}{0.05}=4.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(1.5)^{p+1} & ≈4 \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{1.5}⁡(4) \\ p+1 & ≈3.419… \\ p & ≈2.419….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186443231 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29061ed8-03ee-5954-99b1-36ee8a7d846e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186443105} {:answer/id #uuid "51897522-282c-5afb-8a2d-f610a69ae795" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186443125} {:answer/id #uuid "5751dcbe-8a8b-5270-9916-49268913535f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186443132} {:answer/id #uuid "b1090be2-8599-5d76-a4a0-6edb0f56303b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186443170} {:answer/id #uuid "fd8d57dc-394d-5daa-9001-0b4b29133d6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186443204}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186443132} :answer-field/id #uuid "363cd73d-f05d-5d69-8b42-f72895d3771c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186443208}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "34486fa6-cccf-5fd8-a975-d4b80d4ead78" :question/math-academy-id "q-334545" :question/problem "A numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}+(Δx)^{4}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.6,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.6,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.6) & =4(0.6)^{3}+(0.6)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.216+0.129\,6 \\  & =0.993\,6 \\  & ≈0.994.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =4(0.2)^{3}+(0.2)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.008+0.001\,6 \\  & =0.033\,6 \\  & ≈0.034.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.6$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.6}{0.2}=3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.993\,6$ to $0.033\,6.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.993\,6}{0.033\,6}=29.571\,42…≈29.571.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈29.571\,42… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(29.571\,42…) \\ p+1 & ≈3.083… \\ p & ≈2.083….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$2.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}+(Δx)^{4}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{3})=O\,((Δx)^{2+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186443235 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1629f72c-2b7a-5ad9-9802-4a4c18a43f8a" :answer/type {:db/id {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

First, we compute the GTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.4,$ the GTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}e(0.4) & =5(0.4)^{4}+(0.4)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.0256+1\cdot 0.010\,24 \\  & =0.128+0.010\,24 \\  & =0.138\,24 \\  & ≈0.138.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the GTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}e(0.2) & =5(0.2)^{4}+(0.2)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.0016+1\cdot 0.000\,32 \\  & =0.008+0.000\,32 \\  & =0.008\,32 \\  & ≈0.008.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.4$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.4}{0.2}=2.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p}={2}^{p}.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.138\,24$ to $0.008\,32.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.138\,24}{0.008\,32}=16.615\,384…≈16.615.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{p} & ≈16.615\,384… \\ p & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(16.615\,384…) \\ p & ≈4.054….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the GTE:

$$
e(Δx)=5(Δx)^{4}+(Δx)^{5}\,⇒\,e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{4})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.6,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.6) & =5(0.6)^{4}+3(0.6)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.129\,6+3\cdot 0.077\,76 \\  & =0.648+0.233\,28 \\  & =0.881\,28 \\  & ≈0.881.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.3) & =5(0.3)^{4}+3(0.3)^{5} \\  & =5\cdot 0.008\,1+3\cdot 0.002\,43 \\  & =0.0405+0.007\,29 \\  & =0.047\,79 \\  & ≈0.048.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.6$ to $0.3.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.6}{0.3}=2.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.881\,28$ to $0.047\,79.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.881\,28}{0.047\,79}=18.440\,67…≈18.441.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{p+1} & ≈18.440\,67… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(18.440\,67…) \\ p+1 & ≈4.204… \\ p & ≈3.204….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$3.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=5(Δx)^{4}+3(Δx)^{5}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{4})=O\,((Δx)^{3+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $3.$"} {:db/id 17592186443240 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2292995f-4795-53f0-bb31-0814de610887" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-334564" :question/problem "The global truncation error (GTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
e(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.6,$ the global truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the global truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

{{field-3}}.

{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

First, we compute the GTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.6,$ the GTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}e(0.6) & =6(0.6)^{3}-(0.6)^{4} \\  & =6\cdot 0.216-1\cdot 0.129\,6 \\  & =1.296-0.129\,6 \\  & =1.166\,4 \\  & ≈1.166.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the GTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}e(0.3) & =6(0.3)^{3}-(0.3)^{4} \\  & =6\cdot 0.027-1\cdot 0.008\,1 \\  & =0.162-0.008\,1 \\  & =0.153\,9 \\  & ≈0.154.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.6$ to $0.3.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.6}{0.3}=2.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p}={2}^{p}.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $1.166\,4$ to $0.153\,9.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{1.166\,4}{0.153\,9}=7.578\,94…≈7.579.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{p} & ≈7.578\,94… \\ p & ≈{log}_{2}⁡(7.578\,94…) \\ p & ≈2.922….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$3.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the GTE:

$$
e(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}\,⇒\,e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{3})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $3.$"} {:db/id 17592186443547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33d8185a-6a2a-5892-8eca-d2a40aec6d78" :answer/type {:db/id $r(t)=5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,k,$  $\,t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))k \\  & =5\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,i-4\cdot 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j+3\cdot 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,k \\  & =20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,i-16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j+12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))}^{2}+{(16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))}^{2}+{(12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{400{cos}^{2}⁡(4t)+256{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)+144{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)} \\  & =\sqrt{400[{cos}^{2}⁡(4t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)]} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}20\,\text{d}u \\  & =20u\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =20t\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $s=20t$, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =20t \\ t & =\frac{s}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r\left(\frac{s}{20}\right) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})k \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)k.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443898 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b5588c5-37db-5b02-87d7-05e19f211482" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186443849} {:answer/id #uuid "50a64c5e-ee2e-5e33-99cd-2507a3e15ed4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186443859} {:answer/id #uuid "db8aafa7-86be-5335-ad0b-879f8daf56c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186443882} {:answer/id #uuid "df3fead8-a8d0-5dc8-8d4a-f1f7b93d5a94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{16}" :db/id 17592186443883} {:answer/id #uuid "e9f51edd-60f6-5c7d-8ca5-c07095020041" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186443885}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186443849} :answer-field/id #uuid "92c3c624-d0ce-5d7e-af1f-33bffa533d5b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186443890}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8e84a8d6-a1ed-5f78-832b-753ef57840b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-83657" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where

$$
r(s)=⟨1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right),\,3-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)⟩,\,0\le s<8\pi .
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(3-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right))⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{4},\,-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{4},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{4}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =|\frac{1}{4}|\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right))}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)+{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443899 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c9b736d-97b9-5346-ae4c-3f48e12a4b99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186443857} {:answer/id #uuid "4efce17f-3075-5e92-ad94-a11200baf0b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186443858} {:answer/id #uuid "8d0a7ca2-651b-528e-afe7-bc816f290417" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186443870} {:answer/id #uuid "ac11b4df-2cb6-5f6b-92fb-3e07ba50cb5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186443875} {:answer/id #uuid "c2b8e622-9766-5512-823c-41c899359c51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186443879}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186443857} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2ae9bf6-e514-5558-98b8-e081859740e5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186443894}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "941975f4-ea50-5edb-a299-e8568f71e188" :question/math-academy-id "q-83663" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$ given that its derivative ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the corresponding unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$ are as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=\,-12{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{3})i+12{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,j,\,{T}^{′}(t)=-3{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,i-3{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{3})\,j\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the derivative of the curve ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find the magnitudes of ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${T}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-12{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{3}))}^{2}+{(12{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3}))}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-12{t}^{2})^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡({t}^{3})+(12{t}^{2})^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡({t}^{3})} \\  & =\sqrt{(12{t}^{2})^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡({t}^{3})+{cos}^{2}⁡({t}^{3}))} \\  & =12{t}^{2} \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-3{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3}))}^{2}+{(-3{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{3}))}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3{t}^{2})^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡({t}^{3})+(-3{t}^{2})^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡({t}^{3})} \\  & =\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡({t}^{3})+{cos}^{2}⁡({t}^{3}))} \\  & =3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{3{t}^{2}}{12{t}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2cos)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
